Chapter Summary

Mydei and his incubi familiar as per usual duel, attend some meeting, complete a ritual, and have a totally normal and not caring and soft moment together!

The clash of metal rang through the training hall, a sharp, rhythmic sound that cut through the otherwise silent space. Mydei, Crown Prince of Heaven, moved with precise efficiency, his sword striking with disciplined force. Across from him, Phainon sidestepped effortlessly, dodging each blow with an infuriatingly smooth grace.

“You’re getting predictable, my Prince,” Phainon drawled, smirking as he leaned just out of reach.

Mydei exhaled sharply, his grip tightening on the hilt of his sword. “Focus.”

Phainon grinned. “I am. On you.”

Mydei lunged, and Phainon slipped behind him with a speed that shouldn’t have been possible. A sharp inhale—the feeling of warm breath against his ear—

“You’re stiff today,” Phainon murmured. “Something on your mind?”

Mydei pivoted sharply, but Phainon was already a step ahead, dancing away just out of range. The Incubi’s movements were fluid, teasing, always just brushing the edge of a real fight but never quite engaging seriously. It was infuriating.

“Fight properly,” Mydei snapped.

“But where’s the fun in that?” Phainon countered. He tilted his head, eyes gleaming. “Or are you just frustrated?”

Mydei struck again—faster, more aggressive—but Phainon caught his wrist mid-swing. The sudden proximity sent a spark of irritation down Mydei’s spine. Phainon’s grip was firm but playful, his fingers lingering just a second too long.

“A prince should be more patient,” Phainon mused.

Mydei yanked his arm free. “A familiar should know his place.”

Phainon laughed, stepping back with an easy smile. “Oh, I do. Right by your side. Bound to you, after all.” His gaze flickered, sharp and knowing. “No escaping me, my Prince.”

Mydei turned away before Phainon could see the flicker of frustration in his expression. He sheathed his sword with more force than necessary.

“Training’s over,” he said curtly, striding toward the exit.

“Already?” Phainon called after him, amusement lacing his tone. “But we were just getting started!”

Mydei didn’t look back. He wouldn’t give Phainon the satisfaction of seeing how much he’d gotten under his skin.

Summoning an Incubi was never the plan.

Mydei had been prepared for something grander, something befitting the Crown Prince of Heaven. A celestial beast wreathed in divine fire, perhaps, or a guardian carved from the stars themselves. Instead, the summoning circle flared with deep crimson light, shadows twisting unnaturally before coalescing into a figure lounging at its center, all dark silk and lazy arrogance.

Phainon had tilted his head, blue eyes gleaming with mischief as he took in his surroundings—then took in Mydei.

“You’re not what I expected,” Mydei had said, standing rigid, his disappointment carefully masked behind authority.

Phainon had grinned. “Neither are you.”

The binding had been sealed before Mydei could demand another summoning.

That was years ago, and if Phainon had been a thorn in his side then, he was a whole damn briar patch now.

The training hall remained quiet after Mydei’s departure, save for the faint hum of his sheathed sword. Phainon stretched his arms overhead, rolling his shoulders before sauntering after him.

“You’ll hurt yourself if you keep holding tension like that,” he remarked as he fell into step beside Mydei.

“I’ll hurt you if you keep talking,” Mydei replied flatly.

Phainon chuckled. “Empty threats, my Prince. You’d miss me.”

Mydei refused to dignify that with a response.

As they stepped into the open air, golden light poured over the courtyard, painting the pristine marble in warm hues. It should have been a peaceful sight, but Phainon’s presence was anything but. He was always at Mydei’s side, always lingering at the edges of propriety, always testing the limits of his patience.

And yet—despite himself—Mydei had never once considered breaking their bond.

Phainon sighed dramatically, breaking the silence. “What now? More princely duties? Another round of ‘pretend I don’t want to strangle my familiar’?”

Mydei exhaled slowly. “I have a meeting with the Council.”

Phainon wrinkled his nose. “Boring. No wonder you’re tense.”

“Then leave me be.”

Phainon placed a hand over his heart, feigning injury. “Cruel. And after all the time we’ve spent together.”

Mydei barely spared him a glance. “If only it were less.”

Phainon smirked. “Admit it. You’d be lost without me.”

For once, Mydei didn’t answer.

And that, more than anything, made Phainon pause before following.

The council chamber was a grand hall of polished marble and towering columns, bathed in soft celestial light. Its silence was a thing of order, heavy with decorum and the weight of divine governance.

And then there was Phainon.

He walked beside Mydei with an easy stride, hands loosely tucked behind his head, humming a tune that had no place in the solemnity of the moment. It was a lazy, almost mocking melody, and it did not stop even as they reached the massive doors of the chamber, where two armored sentinels bowed deeply to their Crown Prince.

Phainon winked at them in passing.

Mydei exhaled sharply through his nose. “Must you?”

“Oh? Did you have a song preference?” Phainon asked, tilting his head. “Perhaps something more regal? I could try a ballad—”

“Phainon.”

Phainon grinned. “Fine, fine. I’ll be good.”

Mydei doubted that.

The doors opened, revealing the assembled council—elders of wisdom and power, each draped in flowing robes of celestial white and gold. They turned as one to greet their prince, their expressions serene and composed. But as Phainon strolled in after him, humming louder now, that composure visibly strained.

A few narrowed their eyes. One elder sighed deeply, already resigned. Another, the High Minister, clasped his hands together with long-suffering patience.

“My Prince,” the High Minister greeted, ignoring Phainon entirely. “We are honored by your presence.”

Phainon leaned in slightly. “And mine?”

No one answered.

Mydei sat at the head of the chamber, back straight, gaze firm. Phainon, rather than standing respectfully behind him, leaned against the side of the chair, close enough that Mydei could feel his presence like an ember at his shoulder.

The meeting began. Reports were given on celestial defenses, divine laws, and the state of the heavenly realms. Mydei listened, responding where needed, every bit the composed ruler he was trained to be. And through it all, Phainon remained.

He played with a lock of Mydei’s hair at one point.

Mydei caught his wrist without looking.

Phainon smirked. “Distracting, am I?”

“Do you have a death wish?”

“Would you deliver it personally?”

Mydei tightened his grip slightly before letting go. Phainon chuckled, unfazed, and settled beside him with the ease of someone who had long

since claimed his place at Mydei’s side—whether anyone liked it or not.

The council endured his presence, but as the meeting drew to a close, the High Minister finally addressed the matter.

“My Prince,” he began delicately, “may I suggest that certain company is perhaps… inappropriate for discussions of such importance?”

Phainon feigned a gasp. “Oh, certain company? That wouldn’t be me, would it?”

“Phainon,” Mydei warned.

The Incubi sighed. “Fine, fine. You wound me, Minister, truly. But if you insist, I’ll leave the boring talks to you.” He pushed off the chair and stretched, unbothered. “I’ll be outside, my Prince. Don’t miss me too much.”

With that, he sauntered out, humming again—louder than before.

The council chamber fell into relieved silence.

Mydei pinched the bridge of his nose.

The High Minister cleared his throat. “He remains… an unconventional choice, Your Highness.”

Tell me something I don’t know.

But Mydei only straightened, voice calm. “He is bound to me. That is not something I can change.”

Nor something, he realized, that he would change.

Not anymore.

The moment the council meeting ended, Mydei’s body seemed to deflate, his posture shifting from that of a crown prince to someone who had just survived an exhausting ordeal. He stepped out of the grand chamber and

into the courtyard, the warm light of the celestial sun bathing the marble in golden hues.

He barely got a step in before he saw him.

Phainon was sprawled across the steps leading to the royal gardens, one leg casually thrown over the other, an arm draped across his eyes as though he were taking an afternoon nap.

“Oh, for the love of—” Mydei muttered under his breath.

Phainon didn’t even flinch at his approach, instead raising his voice in a dramatic drawl. “Ah, my Prince. How was the delightful council? Was it everything you dreamed of?”

“Do you really have to do this now?” Mydei bit out, eyes narrowing as he stepped closer.

Phainon peeled his arm from his face and grinned up at him, eyes gleaming. “Oh, don’t be so serious, Mydei. Life is far too short for that.” He sat up slowly, stretching as if he were waking from a luxurious slumber. “I, for one, think you were dazzling in there. All that authority… so many important words. I was enthralled.”

“Mm-hmm,” Mydei muttered, the sarcasm grating at him. “And what are you doing?”

Phainon smiled lazily. “What do you mean? I’m resting.” He looked pointedly at the intricate celestial statues surrounding the garden, his gaze lingering on a particularly grand one of a fallen star warrior. “I find it quite peaceful here. These statues have such character.”

Mydei followed his gaze and immediately regretted it. Phainon was draped over one of the statues in a completely inappropriate manner—his hand was resting on the statue’s base, and he looked like he was about to start a conversation with it.

“I swear, Phainon,” Mydei began, a headache already forming at his temples. “I will have you removed from every sacred space if you don’t stop.”

Phainon just shrugged, flashing him that wicked grin. “Oh, please. The statues love me. I’m giving them a little company, a bit of entertainment. They’ve been standing here for centuries, after all. What’s a few more years of me lounging around?”

Mydei rubbed the bridge of his nose in frustration. “You always find a way to make a mess of things.”

“Mess?” Phainon leaned back with an exaggerated pout. “I’m bringing a little life to the place, is all.” He gave a theatrical glance around. “Would you rather I be bored?”

Before Mydei could respond, Phainon was on his feet again, brushing himself off with exaggerated care. “But I suppose I should stop before you decide to get angry with me again. Wouldn’t want to see that pretty little scowl of yours.” He winked.

Mydei made a noise in the back of his throat, too tired to argue. “Let’s go. I have other matters to attend to.”

Phainon fell into step beside him without question, his hum now quieter but still there, like an echo of something much too carefree for the moment. “You know, you’re lucky you’ve got me. Life would be so boring without me.”

Mydei glanced at him, too weary to argue, and almost smiled despite himself. “I don’t know about that.”

“Oh, come now,” Phainon teased, nudging him playfully. “You’d miss me if I wasn’t here.”

Mydei sighed, already walking faster, but Phainon kept pace effortlessly. “Keep dreaming, Phainon.”

“I do.” Phainon grinned. “Every day.”

The Elysian Gardens were peaceful as always, a serene escape from the political turmoil of the celestial courts. Lush greenery spread across the grounds, and intricate stone pathways wove through towering statues of fallen warriors and celestial beings. The air was filled with the scent of blooming flowers, and the soft sounds of birds echoed in the distance.

Mydei strolled through the gardens, the thoughts of his responsibilities and duties he’d have to take care of today heavy on his shoulders, though his stride was steady and controlled. He often came here to clear his mind, finding solace in the solitude—or at least, he used to.

Today, however, the quiet was interrupted by the sound of small, hesitant footsteps. Looking down, Mydei spotted a young child standing before him, eyes wide with curiosity. The child was dressed in fine garments that indicated their noble lineage, the sigil of a visiting dignitary’s house embroidered on the chest.

“My Prince,” the child said with a polite bow, though they were clearly unsure of how to approach. “I—I hope I’m not disturbing you.”

Mydei raised an eyebrow, but the level of formality in the child’s voice seemed to soften his usual reserve. “Not at all,” he replied smoothly, though his tone was still that of someone unused to children’s presence. “What brings you to the Gardens?”

The child hesitated but then looked up at him with bright eyes. “My mother says I must be on my best behavior while here, but… I wanted to ask if you’d let me braid your hair.”

Mydei blinked, caught off guard by the request. He wasn’t particularly used to such boldness from anyone, let alone a child. His hand instinctively brushed a few strands of hair behind his ear as if checking if it were in disarray.

“I’m afraid my hair is not meant for such things,” Mydei said, his voice still calm but with the barest hint of reluctance.

Phainon, who had been leaning casually against a nearby pillar, watched with an amused glint in his eyes. “I think it could use a little fun,” he mused, loud enough for Mydei to hear but not addressing him directly. “What’s a little braid between you and royalty?”

Mydei shot Phainon a glance but said nothing in reply, his focus still on the child, who looked up at him expectantly.

“Well, if you truly wish,” Mydei said finally, his voice softening just enough to convey that he wasn’t entirely against the idea, “I’ll allow you a single braid. But do it quickly. I have duties to attend to.”

The child’s face lit up with joy, and before Mydei could change his mind, they hurried to his side, gathering the strands of his hair with surprising skill. Mydei stood still, his gaze scanning the serene beauty of the gardens, though his posture remained as composed as ever. He made no move to stop the child, though a hint of amusement flickered in his eyes as the braid slowly took shape.

Phainon couldn’t help but chuckle from his spot by the pillar, arms crossed. “Well, I never thought I’d see the day,” he said, more to himself than to anyone. “The mighty Crown Prince of Heaven…allowing his hair to be braided so willfully, by a child no less.”

Mydei didn’t respond, though the corner of his mouth twitched ever so slightly. The child, oblivious to the underlying tension between the two, hummed softly as they worked, clearly delighted by the opportunity.

Phainon leaned in slightly, his smirk widening. “You know, I could do an even better braid if you’d let me.”

Mydei finally turned his head just enough to fix Phainon with a warning glare. “Don’t push your luck.”

Phainon grinned but held up his hands in mock surrender. “Fine, fine. I’ll let the kid have this victory.”

The child finished tying off the braid with a small ribbon from their sleeve and stepped back, beaming with pride. “There! Now you look even more regal, Your Highness!”

Mydei reached up, fingers brushing over the braid, his expression unreadable. “Hmph,” was all he said, but the sharp edges of his usual demeanor seemed to soften, just a little.

Phainon tilted his head, watching Mydei with something unreadable in his own gaze. “Well, well,” he murmured. “Would you look at that.”

Mydei ignored him. “Go on now,” he told the child, his voice gentler than before. “Your mother will be looking for you.”

The child bowed deeply before scampering off, leaving Mydei standing in the sunlight, the single braid a quiet testament to the rare moment of indulgence.

Phainon, watching him closely, smiled—not in his usual teasing way, but something quieter, something thoughtful.

“Regal, huh?” he mused, mostly to himself.

Mydei finally turned his attention back to him. “Not a word,” he warned.

Phainon merely chuckled, falling into step beside him as they left the gardens. “Oh, my Prince,” he drawled, eyes twinkling with mischief. “This is going to haunt you forever.”

Mydei didn’t disagree with that.

Okhema was a city of light. That was its virtue, its pride—stone kissed by divinity, prayers woven into the air itself. It reeked of sanctity, the scent

cloying, thick, and layered with something sickly sweet to Phainon’s senses. He hated it. He loved it.

If there was ever a place that tempted corruption, it was this one.

Phainon walked a step behind Mydei, not because he was obligated to but because it was safer that way. The prince strode through the marble streets with the same cold poise as always, indifferent to the awed and reverent gazes that followed him. People whispered in his wake, hands pressed to their chests in respect. Here, Mydei was seen as a celestial force, a prince of the divine. Phainon, trailing behind him, felt like something dredged up from the dark.

It thrilled him.

He grinned, tongue sliding over his teeth, catching the sharp points. No one here knew. No one understood what he was, what he could do if he wanted to. The weight of devotion, the raw emotion that saturated the air, made his skin hum, his hunger twisting deep in his core. It was a slow, aching pulse, something he had mastered the art of ignoring. But here, in Okhema, where desire was wrapped in faith, where people surrendered themselves so easily to something greater than them—Phainon could barely breathe.

He should leave.

He wouldn’t.

Not when Mydei moved like that, purposeful and untouchable, his presence cutting through the city’s purity like a blade. Phainon’s fingers twitched. He wanted to touch him, wanted to press up against him just to feel if that unwavering composure would crack, if Mydei’s pulse would jump beneath his palm. The thought sent a slow, molten curl of something wicked through him.

“Behave yourself,” Mydei said suddenly, not looking back.

Phainon chuckled, low and dark. “What am I doing?”

“You’re thinking too loudly.”

That was dangerous. But then again, so was he.

They passed a group of acolytes kneeling in prayer, their lips moving in soft, reverent murmurs. Phainon’s gaze dragged over them, lingering where robes dipped, where skin flushed from the midday heat. He could taste it, the hints of want buried beneath devotion. It would be so easy. Just a touch. A whisper. The right kind of temptation, and they’d fall into his hands like ripe fruit.

A sharp, silent warning cut through his thoughts—Mydei’s fingers brushing against his wrist, a fleeting, deliberate touch. Phainon inhaled sharply, heat curling low in his gut. Mydei didn’t even glance at him.

“Don’t test me,” the prince murmured.

Phainon exhaled, laughter caught somewhere between frustration and delight. “Never.”

Liar.

The night deepened, and Okhema’s nightlife hummed softly, distant murmurs drifting on the breeze as Mydei and Phainon ventured into the quieter, darker corners of the city. The streets here carried an unsettling silence, as though even the air itself was holding its breath. It was in this eerie stillness that Phainon’s restraint, already frayed by the weight of the city, finally unraveled.

Mydei halted before an ancient temple, its golden doors etched with intricate, divine patterns. He turned to Phainon, his tone as steady as ever. “We’ll be staying here for the night. I need time to—”

But Phainon was already moving. His expression shifted, no longer the playful tease, but something darker, something far more dangerous. He hadn’t meant to—hadn’t planned it—but Okhema’s intoxicating pull, its

suffocating devotion, the way every breath seemed heavy with emotion… He couldn’t stand it any longer.

He turned to face Mydei, his eyes burning with a hunger that was impossible to disguise now. The teasing, the games, all fell away. “Do you feel it, Mydei?” His voice dropped to a low rasp, dangerous and charged with a potency that seemed to vibrate through the very air. “This city… the way it calls to us. How easy it would be to lose ourselves in it. If you let me.”

Mydei froze, sensing the shift immediately. It wasn’t his Phainon anymore. No, the darkness that had always lurked beneath the surface was creeping out, his true nature slipping through, thick and primal.

Phainon closed the distance between them, each step deliberate, the tension thickening in the air. His breath, warm and insistent, brushed against Mydei’s skin, and Mydei’s pulse jumped. It felt like the world had narrowed to just the two of them, the space between them charged with something too dangerous to name. Phainon leaned in, his lips grazing the delicate shell of Mydei’s ear. “I could give you what you truly desire,” he whispered, the words heavy with promise, but also a subtle, threatening edge.

For a moment, the distance between them seemed to collapse entirely. Phainon’s presence enveloped Mydei, making the air feel suffocating, taut with unspoken things. His lips were so close, his body too near, and yet the words hung there, the invitation impossible to ignore.

But Mydei wasn’t one to easily fall prey to temptation, especially not when he knew just how deep this pull was, how dangerous. His hand shot out, seizing Phainon’s wrist with a force that was almost violent. “Enough.”

The word sliced through the thick tension, and in that moment, the air seemed to snap—like the stillness of the night had been cracked open by something primal.

The chill of the night seemed to sharpen as Phainon stepped back, his breath coming unevenly. He hadn’t meant to lose control—not like this, not

in front of Mydei. His usual confidence faltered, but he wasn’t about to grovel. He simply… regretted it.

“I’m sorry,” he said, his voice steady but carrying a faint undercurrent of something darker—shaken at the unusual loss of control, but not broken. “I crossed a line.”

His eyes remained fixed on the ground, avoiding Mydei’s gaze. The last thing he needed was to see the prince’s reaction, to read something in his eyes that would drag him back into that maddening pull.

Mydei stood still, silent. It was almost unbearable. The air between them hummed with unspoken thoughts, yet no words followed.

Phainon took a slow breath, his hands curling into fists at his sides, forcing himself to remain composed. “I’ll… keep my distance.” The words hung there, an offering and an apology in one.

The silence stretched on. For a moment, it felt like everything was held in suspension—the tension thickening with every passing second, both of them feeling it, but neither willing to speak further.

Mydei finally spoke, his voice quiet, but clear. “Don’t make promises you can’t keep.”

Phainon’s jaw tightened, and for a moment, he considered turning away, leaving, but the thought vanished as quickly as it came. He couldn’t leave Mydei here, not like this. With a sharp exhale, he followed a few paces behind the prince, his gaze still lowered, keeping a respectful distance. His thoughts churned, and the fire that had sparked in him earlier was now buried deep beneath layers of control.

Mydei kept walking, unfazed, but Phainon could sense that the prince was aware of the shift, the uncomfortable tension that had settled in.

Phainon’s hands curled tighter into fists at his sides as he followed, keeping his distance but not leaving. He’d stay with Mydei, no matter the silence.

The golden doors of the temple loomed ahead, opening with an unsettling creak. Inside, the air was heavy with incense and the quiet hum of prayers. The flickering light of candles danced on the walls, casting long shadows, and at the far end of the temple stood the Tribios—Tribbie, Trianne, and Trinnon—waiting patiently.

As always, they resembled children despite their age, their features perfectly identical, and their strange mannerisms further evoking that childlike innocence. They wore pale robes that fluttered like the wings of ghosts, and their eyes, sharp yet innocent, glimmered as Mydei entered.

“Dei,” they chorused in unison, their voices as sweet as they were eerie. “We’ve been expecting you.”

Phainon, ever the observer, leaned casually against one of the marble pillars, arms crossed, a grin tugging at the corner of his lips as he watched them. The Tribios always had this effect on him—he could never bring himself to act teasingly with them. They reminded him too much of younger siblings, and in turn, he was incredibly endeared by their antics. They had a way of making him feel simultaneously grounded and unsettled.

“You’re late,” Tribbie remarked, her eyes flicking over to Phainon. “We’ve been waiting for both of you. Snowy…” She trailed off, a small smirk forming as she looked at him.

Phainon’s eyes sparkled with mischief. “I wasn’t the one holding us up,” he said with mock indignation. “Mydei’s busy being all important and princely.”

Mydei shot Phainon a half-glare, but Phainon only winked in return. He could never resist teasing, especially when it came to Mydei. The air between them was always ripe for it.

“Don’t make this harder than it is,” Mydei muttered under his breath, clearly not amused.

The Tribios exchanged a glance, their childlike giggles echoing softly in the temple. “We have a ritual tonight,” Trianne said, stepping forward with an unsettling grace. “A purification, a cleansing of the soul. It will require you both to focus and trust in the process.”

Phainon raised an eyebrow, his grin widening. “Purification, huh?” His tone was light, but there was an edge to it. He was, after all, an Incubi— temptation was his domain. “What’s the catch? No getting possessed or anything, right?” He said this as if he hasn’t gone through it thousand of times.

The Tribios smiled serenely, unfazed by his sarcasm, and indulging him. “No catch. Only your trust. You will be tested—both of you.”

Phainon’s gaze flickered to Mydei, who appeared unperturbed as always. Mydei might be the one in charge of the kingdom, but in here, in Okhema’s sacred space, even he had to abide by the temple’s rules.

Phainon pushed himself off the pillar, his grin still present but his voice quieter. “All right, let’s see what you’ve got for us.” His teasing demeanor remained, but there was a flicker of curiosity, a desire to see what this ritual would reveal.

The Tribios nodded, and with a swish of their robes, they moved to prepare the ritual space. Phainon and Mydei stood at the center, the air thick with an energy that Phainon could almost taste.

“Ready for this?” Phainon murmured to Mydei, not looking at him but at the silent preparation in front of them.

Mydei gave a slight nod. “We don’t have much choice, do we?”

Phainon chuckled lightly. “I’m just wondering what kind of trouble I’m going to get into.” He then turned his gaze toward the Tribios, eyes glinting with amusement. “Lead the way, kids.”

Despite his playful tone, there was an underlying wariness to his posture. He was more attuned to the strange, dark energy swirling around them than

Mydei was. But for now, he stayed silent, watching the Tribios prepare for the ritual was about to take place.

Despite the playful banter, there was a subtle wariness to Phainon’s posture. His body was on alert, attuned to the strange, unsettling energy that seemed to cling to the air around them. He could feel it—the tension in the very air, the sacred power of purification that would soon course through the temple. While Mydei remained mostly unaffected, Phainon felt every pulse of that energy like a whisper to his very core.

The ritual wasn’t something he wanted to endure, but it was part of his bond with Mydei. As his familiar, Phainon had to be present, had to endure the process alongside the prince. It wasn’t just tradition—it was a requirement. One that would leave him weakened and vulnerable, but still, it was necessary. If Phainon wanted to remain bound to Mydei, he couldn’t refuse this. Not even for his own sanity.

He stayed silent as the Tribios began their preparations, the young high priests moving with practiced ease, their small forms somehow radiating an aura of ancient power. Phainon’s eyes darted between them and the temple’s vast, hallowed walls, his mind focused on the ritual about to unfold. Despite his lighthearted remarks, his body tensed with anticipation. This would be painful. And the aftermath? Far worse.

But for Mydei, Phainon would endure it—no matter how much it cost him.

The temple was silent, save for the soft hum of the Tribios’ chant. The air grew heavier with each passing second, saturated with a divine energy that burned like fire and pressed down like stone. The purification was already beginning. The golden light around them flickered, intense and sharp. It was a force that Phainon would never become accustomed to, one that seared through his very being. And Mydei knew it.

Phainon had long since given up pretending to be unaffected. He clenched his jaw, his hands trembling as he fought to stay on his feet. He could feel the burn starting deep in his chest, the way the light tugged at his soul, trying to rid him of everything that made him what he was. The purity it demanded was something that could never be his. Not entirely.

The Tribios’ voices rose in unison, their words creating a sonic web of divinity that crushed down on Phainon’s mind. The light enveloped him, and every nerve in his body screamed in protest. But even as his limbs began to tremble, even as his vision blurred and his breath came in ragged gasps, Phainon refused to let himself collapse. Not in front of Mydei.

The prince, standing beside him, was silent but tense, his gaze fixed on Phainon with an expression that was equal parts concern and something darker, guilt mingling with helplessness. Mydei’s fingers twitched, as if reaching for Phainon, but he didn’t move. He knew what the ritual demanded. He knew what it cost Phainon. Yet there was nothing he could do to stop it.

“You know this is necessary,” Mydei said quietly, his voice threaded with remorse, but resolute. “For both of us.”

Phainon could barely hear him over the deafening pulse of divine energy, but the words cut through nonetheless. His lips curled into something that could have been a smile, but it was more a grimace. “Necessary… sure,” he rasped. “But I never said I liked it.”

Mydei winced, the guilt deepening in his chest. He knew. He could feel it— the suffering Phainon was enduring. The prince had seen it too many times over the centuries. Every time the purification took place, he had to watch as his familiar was burned from the inside out, his demonic essence stripped away by the purity of the ritual. It left Phainon weakened, barely able to stand, and it never failed to eat away at Mydei’s insides. But it had to be done.

The Tribios continued their chant, and Phainon’s body buckled slightly under the strain. His breath was shallow, but he held his ground. It was almost unbearable. He could feel his essence crumbling under the weight of the holy light, his incubi nature fighting back, desperately trying to resist.

“Stay with me, Snowy,” Mydei murmured, his voice low, almost pleading, but his eyes never left Phainon’s face. The prince wasn’t sure if he was speaking to Phainon for reassurance or for himself.

Phainon swallowed hard, his eyes flickering as he forced his gaze up to Mydei, offering him a half-hearted grin. “What, you think I’m going to collapse in front of you?” His voice was weak, strained, but there was something about his bravado that made Mydei’s heart tighten in his chest.

“I know you’re strong,” Mydei said, barely louder than a whisper. “But I also know how much this hurts.”

It wasn’t long before the ritual reached its apex. The Tribios’ voices blended into a single, resonant note, and Phainon couldn’t hold back anymore. His knees buckled under the intensity, and his chest heaved in ragged breaths. He felt as if he were being torn apart, his very identity sundered by the light. His head spun, his vision darkening at the edges, and he could taste the metallic tang of blood in his mouth.

Finally, the ritual ended. The light receded, leaving Phainon trembling in its wake. His body, frail and exhausted, was barely able to stand, but he did— barely. His head lolled to the side, sweat dripping down his brow, and his breath came in shallow gasps.

The Tribios stepped back, their eyes shining with satisfaction, and they muttered something in unison that Phainon couldn’t catch. He was barely aware of them now, his senses dulling. The ritual had stripped him of everything that made him who he was, and he felt exposed, vulnerable.

But the worst part was that Mydei had watched it all.

Without another word, Mydei moved toward Phainon, his hand gently but firmly guiding him away from the center of the ritual. The Tribios stepped aside as the prince passed, their faces unreadable, but their gazes following them with a silent intensity. Despite their childlike appearances, there was something ancient and knowing about the way they watched the pair leave.

“Take care of him, Dei,” Tribbie called softly, her voice a blend of innocence and something far older.

“We hope the journey is kinder to you, Snowy,” Trianne added, her tone carrying a note of quiet concern.

Trinnon gave a faint nod, but said nothing, his amber eyes lingering on Phainon with a strange, solemn air.

Mydei didn’t reply to them. He simply nodded, acknowledging their presence before guiding Phainon out of the temple. The air outside was colder than it had been inside, and the night pressed in with its silence as they left the ritual chamber behind. Phainon leaned heavily on Mydei, every step a struggle, though he didn’t protest.

“Mydei…” Phainon murmured, his voice strained. He tried to push himself upright, but the effort was futile. “I’ll be fine.” It was the same line he always said, even when he knew it wasn’t true.

Mydei didn’t respond, but his grip tightened on Phainon’s arm. His expression was unreadable, though the way his jaw tightened suggested something darker was stirring beneath the surface. He didn’t need to say it out loud—the guilt that always followed these rituals hung between them, suffocating and unspoken.

Phainon, exhausted and trembling, was too worn to speak. His mind drifted, the pain from the ritual lingering, gnawing at him. But Mydei was here. Mydei always was.

They passed through the temple doors, the cool night air cutting against Phainon’s flushed skin, offering a brief sense of relief from the suffocating pain. But that relief was fleeting, and the tremors in Phainon’s body only deepened as the ritual’s effects lingered. Mydei glanced at him, his fingers tightening on Phainon’s arm in silent reassurance.

“We’ll get you some rest,” Mydei said, his voice low and determined. “Just a little longer.”

Phainon didn’t reply. There was no need to. Mydei always took care of him when this happened—whether Phainon liked it or not.

Mydei’s grip on Phainon tightened as the exhausted Incubi leaned heavily on him. The tremors running through Phainon were a cruel reminder of

what he had just endured. Each step was labored, but Mydei didn’t rush him. He had seen this before. He had done this before.

“Just hold on a little longer,” Mydei murmured, his voice soft but firm, though his eyes betrayed the guilt that had followed him for centuries.

Phainon could barely register the words, his body too worn to care. His mind was foggy, his senses dulled by the pain. But his instincts, his hunger, they were already starting to wake up.

They reached a secluded part of the city, away from the watchful eyes of the temple, the cold night air pressing in on them. Mydei’s pace slowed as they approached a stone archway hidden in the shadows.

“This way,” Mydei said quietly, his voice barely above a whisper as he guided Phainon forward. The air around them thickened, a palpable sense of magic swirling in the air. Mydei’s blood pulsed beneath his skin—its signature was unmistakable. This was the passage, a thin seam between dimensions, a place neither here nor there, where time twisted and reality bent.

Phainon, his gaze unfocused and hazy, took in the dark archway, sensing something familiar but distant in the air.

“You know this place,” Mydei said with a small sigh, the words more to himself than to Phainon. “This is where you go after. Where you always go.”

Phainon’s eyes flickered, barely registering his words. The hunger inside him was too loud, too demanding.

Mydei, in a practiced motion, pricked his own finger with a small, delicate blade. Blood pooled at the tip, dark and thick, and he pressed it against the stone, muttering words in a language Phainon couldn’t quite place. The air rippled as the passage opened, a tear in the fabric of reality itself.

Without a word, Mydei led Phainon through.

The world on the other side was nothing like Okhema, or anything Phainon had seen before. It was a hellish, desolate place. A vast, endless void stretched out in all directions, filled with wailing souls trapped in eternal torment. Their cries echoed through the expanse, and the ground was littered with debris—broken, twisted remnants of lives long past. The air was thick, oppressive, suffocating, a stark contrast to the purity of Okhema.

Phainon’s body reacted before his mind could catch up. The hunger, the sharp, insatiable thirst, took over in an instant. He pulled away from Mydei, his senses zeroing in on the lost souls around them. His eyes glowed faintly, a wicked smile curling on his lips.

Without a word, he lunged, tearing into the closest soul with all the ferocity of a predator. Blood—dark, black, and thick—spilled around him as he tore and devoured. The air around him seemed to hum, the power of the souls feeding him, invigorating him. Phainon reveled in the release, the freedom to feast without restraint, without concern for the consequences.

Mydei stood back, his gaze lingering on Phainon’s frenzied movements. The prince’s face remained impassive, though the faintest hint of sorrow seemed to linger in his eyes. He had brought Phainon here for centuries, and though he knew the cost, it didn’t matter. Not anymore.

Phainon was in his element now, a true demon—a force of nature unleashed. Mydei, as always, looked away, refusing to watch what Phainon became during these moments.

The corruption of Phainon didn’t concern him—not really. He couldn’t afford to care. Not when this was the only way to ease the pain of purification. Phainon had to suffer, and if that meant being dragged into this hellish place after every ritual, then so be it. Mydei had long since resigned himself to it.

The prince stood in silence as Phainon tore into the souls, the blood staining the ground, the sounds of his feeding echoing in the endless void. Every cry, every plea for mercy, was drowned out by the frantic energy of the Incubi’s hunger.

When the feeding finally stopped, Phainon was left panting, exhausted, covered in the remains of those he had devoured. His body trembled, but the hunger was gone for now.

Mydei moved to his side, offering a hand to help him up, his face unreadable.

“Ready to go back?” Mydei asked, his voice low.

Phainon nodded weakly, his breath still coming in ragged gasps, his eyes glazed and distant. “Yeah… just… give me a minute.”

Without another word, Mydei led Phainon back through the passage, away from the souls, back to their own world. The air felt different now, less oppressive, but still heavy with the weight of everything they had just endured.

It had become their routine, an unspoken agreement: purification for Mydei, suffering for Phainon, and feeding in a place where the corruption could stretch its tendrils even further in both of them, even Mydei to keep the other living. It was a cycle they had lived with for centuries.

And Mydei, despite the weight of it all, would carry it for as long as he had to.

After Phainon was cleaned up and dressed in loose, comfortable clothes, Mydei led him back to his chambers. The exhaustion from the ritual weighed heavily on the Incubi, his steps slow and unsteady as Mydei supported him. Once inside the chambers, Mydei helped him to the bed and settled him under the covers. Phainon’s breathing was shallow but steady now, his body sinking into the softness of the sheets as his mind slowly relaxed.

Mydei slipped into the bed beside him, pulling the covers up over them both. He let out a long, almost imperceptible sigh as he closed his eyes, trying to unwind after the endless routine. It was a quiet, still moment—one that felt too rare to be fully enjoyed. His mind replayed the purification and

its lingering effects, the guilt gnawing at him. But for now, he pushed it aside, letting the warmth of Phainon’s body next to him be a small comfort in the chaos they both lived in.

Phainon, though exhausted, shifted slightly in his sleep, his face nuzzling into Mydei’s neck. The warmth of his breath against Mydei’s skin was soothing, though a little too intimate. For a moment, Mydei thought it might be the aftermath of the feeding—how touch-starved Phainon was after enduring the pain of the ritual.

Then, unexpectedly, he felt something else. A pressure against his neck, followed by a sharp, sudden sensation as Phainon bit into it.

Mydei’s body tensed immediately, his breath hitching in his throat as he froze. He hadn’t expected this, not in the quiet aftermath of everything they had just been through. The bite was sharp and intentional, Phainon’s teeth sinking into his skin in a way that sent a shiver down Mydei’s spine.

Before Mydei could react, Phainon moved with surprising strength, rolling on top of him. Mydei was momentarily stunned by the shift, the sudden weight of the Incubi pinning him to the bed. He opened his mouth to speak, to ask what was happening, but the words died in his throat as Phainon whispered against his ear.

“I’ll do anything you want after this, Dei… just let me indulge a little longer.”

The warmth of Phainon’s breath against his ear sent another shiver through Mydei, and before he could think, Phainon’s lips were on his neck again. The Incubi’s hands roamed, his touch growing more possessive, teasing as it moved lower and lower down Mydei’s body. He could feel the hunger in the other’s actions, the desperate need that had been kept in check for far too long.

Mydei’s heart raced. The situation felt foreign, uncharted, and for a moment, he had no idea how to navigate it. His breath came out in soft gasps as Phainon’s mouth worked its way down to his collarbone, sucking,

nibbling. Mydei shifted, his body instinctively trying to pull away—but Phainon’s hands were firm, his grip unyielding.

“Phainon…” Mydei managed to say, his voice low, but his tone betraying a hint of nervousness. “Stop…” He hadn’t meant for the command to come out as a breathless whisper, but it did, laced with a tinge of something he couldn’t quite place.

Phainon paused, his lips still lingering at Mydei’s neck, his breath hot against his skin. His eyes, though heavy with exhaustion, glinted with a dark, knowing hunger that set Mydei’s pulse racing.

“I’m sorry, Mydei,” Phainon whispered softly, but his tone was anything but apologetic. It was more like a plea, the softness of the words contradicting the intensity of the actions. He looked at Mydei then, searching his eyes for some kind of permission, or perhaps an understanding.

But Mydei didn’t want this, not right now. Not after everything that had just happened. He reached up, gently cupping Phainon’s jaw, and with surprising gentleness, he guided the Incubi’s head away from his neck.

Phainon let out a soft sigh of frustration, but he didn’t push further. Instead, he settled back against Mydei’s chest, curling into him with a quiet, exhausted murmur. Within moments, the tension in his body relaxed, his breath evening out as he fell into a deep, untroubled sleep.

Mydei, on the other hand, stayed awake long after, his thoughts swirling as he stared at the ceiling, the weight of everything pressing down on him again. He couldn’t help but wonder where the line was, where the end of this routine would lead them. How far would they go before everything they had became too much to bear?

But for now, all he could do was lie there, feeling Phainon’s weight against him, the heat of his body a constant reminder of their bond—one that seemed to grow more complicated by the day.

The morning in the Celestial Realm was never truly morning—it was light eternal, shifting in hues but never fading. Dawn unfolded in gilded tones, brushing across the high spires and endless stretches of sky. It was a world sculpted from divinity, a kingdom untouched by mortal frailty.

And yet, within the sanctum of Mydei’s chambers, the scene was far less grand.

Phainon sprawled across the bed, limbs draped over silk sheets, lazily stretching as if he had all the time in the world. He had regained his strength—no, he had more than regained it. Mydei’s blood worked wonders, mending him from the inside out, and now he was back to his usual self, eyes gleaming with something both knowing and mischievous.

Meanwhile, Mydei stood near the arched windows, already dressed, his presence composed as ever. The faint shimmer of his divinity pulsed with the celestial air, an unspoken authority laced into his very existence. Even in stillness, he was something untouchable.

Phainon, however, didn’t seem impressed.

“Must you always be so diligent first thing in the morning?” he drawled, voice thick with sleep but carrying its usual teasing lilt. “You make the rest of us look bad.”

Mydei didn’t glance his way. “You do that well enough on your own.”

Phainon smirked, rolling onto his side, propping his head up with one hand. “Harsh. What’s the occasion? Another grand celestial decree? Smite some sinners? Or is it just another day of being His Radiance, Crown Prince of the Heavens?”

Mydei turned then, slow and deliberate. “Get up.”

Phainon hummed, tilting his head. “That wasn’t an answer.”

“I wasn’t offering one.”

Phainon sighed theatrically, shifting but making no real move to rise. “Give me a reason.”

Mydei stepped forward, and for a moment, something heavier settled between them—an unspoken expectation, a reminder of who Mydei was outside these chambers. Outside their moments of familiarity.

Then, just as easily, the tension shattered.

“You’ve had more than enough time to lounge,” Mydei said flatly. “Unless you’d like to go another round in purification.”

Phainon was up before the words had fully left Mydei’s lips.

“Well, when you put it like that,” he muttered, stretching once more, a slow, languid motion before he straightened. His smirk returned, effortless. “Fine, fine. Lead the way, Your Radiance.”

Mydei gave him a look.

Phainon grinned, unfazed. Some things never changed.

Chapter Summary

Phainon and Mydei: handling celestial disputes, testing boundaries, and navigating an unspoken tension—all in a day’s work.

Chapter Notes

Again shorter than usual, but I legit forgot the plot I had going on with this cause I didn’t write the outline so I just blazed through it.

I’ve pretty much given up on trying to remember so it’s just gonna be really self-indulgent and whatever comes in my head first I’ll write, fingers crossed you guys will like it🤞

(For some reason I also can’t back read without getting embarrassed so there is also that😭)

The assembly chamber stood in silence.

It was a place of celestial law—vast, towering, woven from light and stone older than mortal understanding. The air itself was thick with judgment, settling over the gathered deities like an unseen hand pressing them into place. The ones before Mydei were not mortals, nor were they weak. And yet, before him, they hesitated.

He did not raise his voice. He never needed to.

The warring deities had called for arbitration, their dispute dragging on for decades. Even here, even now, their pride kept them bristling, shoulders squared, eyes darting toward him as if daring him to choose a side. But Mydei remained still, gaze sweeping across them, letting their grievances crumble under his silence.

“You forget yourselves.”

The words were quiet, but they cut through the chamber like a blade.

A ripple of something unspoken passed through the gathered gods. Even the most indignant among them stilled.

There was no anger in Mydei’s expression, no outward show of force, only the simple, undeniable truth—there was no argument here that could stand against him.

Phainon watched from the marble steps, lounging against a pillar.

It was almost cruel in a way, how easily Mydei unraveled them. Not through fury, not through threats—just sheer certainty.

One of the deities dared to speak. “You cannot expect us to—”

Mydei turned his head.

The deity fell silent mid-sentence, their throat working around a sound that never quite escaped. They looked away.

Phainon exhaled a quiet laugh, tilting his head, watching Mydei as one might admire a rare spectacle. It wasn’t just power—it was the complete absence of doubt. No hesitation, no missteps. It was intoxicating in its own way.

And yet…

Phainon’s gaze flicked toward the gathered celestials, where something far less composed stirred beneath their polished exteriors.

Their reverence was real, but beneath it, there was unease.

And where there was unease, there was want.

He felt it coil beneath the surface, deep-seated and carefully buried— repressed desire, urges they would never dare acknowledge, let alone act

on. It took no effort at all to feel the shift in the chamber as he let his presence unfurl, subtle at first, then pressing, sinking under their skin.

He could taste it.

A celestial attendant’s breath hitched, their fingers flexing against the folds of their robes. Another deity’s pulse stuttered, gaze flicking to him before snapping away too quickly, as if looking for too long was dangerous.

Oh, they knew.

Knew what he was, knew what he could offer, knew exactly how easily he could coax out the things they tried so desperately to bury.

Phainon let his stance loosen, a slow, languid stretch, letting his smirk sharpen just enough. He didn’t even need to speak.

And that made it worse.

A god across the chamber swallowed hard, the movement barely perceptible, but Phainon felt it, felt their barely-contained revulsion twisting with something else—something they’d never admit.

They hated him. Feared him.

But none of them could ignore him.

And Mydei?

He let it happen.

He did nothing to dismiss him, said nothing to break the moment. As if daring them to object.

No one did.

With the dispute settled—at least for now—Mydei remained, speaking with those who required his judgment, finalizing what needed to be done. His

voice was calm, decisive, and unwavering, and though Phainon had long since grown used to it, the effect on others was something else entirely.

He strolled away from the main gathering, his fingers skimming over gilded balustrades, the cool touch of celestial metal humming faintly beneath his skin. Mydei’s presence still filled the chamber, commanding, absolute—and Phainon felt the responses it drew.

It wasn’t just reverence.

He caught it in stolen glances, in barely contained breaths, in the way certain deities held themselves just a little too still, as if suppressing something improper. He didn’t even need to try to sense it—desire, deeply buried, gnawed at the edges of their restraint.

It was amusing, in a way. Even in a place where virtue reigned supreme, no one was immune.

Not even him.

Phainon exhaled slowly, rolling his shoulders in an attempt to shake off the tension curling along his spine. He felt this way too often these days. Mydei’s presence had always had an effect—he’d known that for centuries —but lately, it was getting harder to ignore.

Suppressing a groan, he dragged a hand through his hair and kept walking.

That was when he noticed her.

A woman stood at the periphery of the chamber, wreathed in cool blue light. She wasn’t some lesser celestial, no minor goddess or nameless attendant. No, she was something old.

And her soul smelled delicious.

Phainon’s smirk curled, slow and deliberate, as he made his way toward her.

“You’re new,” he murmured, voice dipping into something smooth and knowing. He let his gaze trail over her, taking his time. “Or at least, new

here.”

She glanced at him, unimpressed at first—until recognition flickered behind her gaze.

“Ah,” she said, tilting her head. “The incubus.”

Phainon grinned. “Caught on quick, have you?”

Her lips curved slightly, something unreadable in her expression. “You reek of indulgence.”

“And you,” Phainon murmured, stepping just a little closer, “reek of restraint.”

Her eyes darkened.

Oh, this would be fun.

-

The last of the celestial squabbles had been settled—at least for now. The echoes of whispered arguments, the tension that had filled the air, all dissipated under Mydei’s unwavering resolve. He stood still for a moment, his mind clearing, the weight of his duties pressing down upon him for only the briefest of moments. He exhaled, the faintest hint of irritation tugging at his thoughts.

This was never how he wanted to spend his time. Celestial disputes, petty squabbles over dominions and power—he’d heard them all before, and honestly, the entire charade wore on him more than he cared to admit. But, as Crown Prince, he had a role to fulfill, and it was one he could not escape.

Still, a part of him longed for the quiet, the simplicity of solitude. Something that, oddly, had become increasingly harder to find.

His gaze swept across the chamber, searching for the presence he had come to expect. Phainon.

He wasn’t there.

A brief flicker of something twisted in his chest. A moment of unease that he quickly buried.

Two possibilities crossed his mind—one, Phainon had simply decided to leave. Wander off and amuse himself, as was his nature. But the second…

Mydei exhaled, refusing to let that thought solidify. The second option was something he didn’t want to think about, something that lingered too close to discomfort.

So, he let it go, and forced himself to focus on the more pressing matters. He would deal with Phainon later. Or perhaps, he wouldn’t—he wasn’t sure which was more appealing at the moment.

Regardless, the room now felt empty without him. And for a fleeting moment, Mydei found himself longing for the presence he’d rather ignore.

The long hall was dim, lit only by faint, glowing lanterns that swayed with the passing wind, their flickering light casting shifting shadows across the marble floor. The soft, rhythmic hum of music filled the air, the performers skillfully moving through their routine, but Mydei wasn’t paying attention. He rarely did when he was forced to sit through these rituals, these grand performances meant to entertain the high-ranking beings in the realm. He was here out of obligation, his presence a formality, but the event wasn’t engaging enough to distract him from the weight of his thoughts.

He leaned back, legs spread wide across the high-backed chair, his posture as comfortable as it was commanding. His robes settled over his thighs, the fabric loose and relaxed, allowing him to sit how he wanted without concern for appearances. His gaze remained distant, staring at the performers with no real interest as his mind wandered, reflecting on things both mundane and important.

Suddenly, the atmosphere shifted.

A presence moved behind him, warm and familiar, and Mydei knew before the whispered voice reached his ear that it was Phainon.

“Mydei,” Phainon’s voice was low, dripping with playful amusement, as he leaned in close. “You miss me?”

The familiar weight of the incubi’s breath sent a brief shiver down Mydei’s spine, though he refused to let it show. He didn’t respond immediately, unwilling to engage with the teasing tone, but Phainon wasn’t one to take silence as rejection.

Before Mydei could turn around, Phainon was already making himself at home—on Mydei’s lap. His body settled with an ease that suggested he had done this a thousand times before, his legs draping lazily over Mydei’s, his head resting comfortably against his chest.

The scene didn’t raise any eyebrows. It never did anymore. Those in the room—beings of great status and stature—had long since learned that Mydei’s familiarity with the incubi wasn’t something to be questioned. Not that any of them dared to.

Phainon let out a soft hum of satisfaction as he adjusted himself, comfortable in the space. His fingers trailed lazily over Mydei’s thigh, sending a ripple of warmth through the prince’s body. Mydei, still half-absorbed in the quiet performance in front of him, didn’t immediately move. There was no need. It was easier this way.

“Must you always be this… relaxed?” Mydei finally said, his voice laced with a quiet edge, though it didn’t carry the sharpness it once had.

Phainon smiled up at him, a playful glint in his eyes. “What can I say? I’m comfortable.” His hands wandered down a little further, fingers teasingly brushing the hem of Mydei’s robes.

For a moment, there was a strange stillness. The noise of the performance seemed far away, muted by the intensity of Phainon’s presence. Mydei’s gaze faltered just briefly, before he straightened his posture, ignoring the subtle pulse of warmth that began to bloom in his chest. His hands, which

had rested loosely at his sides, now adjusted their grip, fingers curled slightly into the fabric of his seat.

It was in that moment that a memory flickered to life, unbidden, from a time long past.

It hadn’t been nearly as easy the first time.

Mydei had been sitting in this very hall, though it had been a different performance then—a gathering full of deities, powerfully adorned and full of self-importance. He had been younger then, more rigid, still trying to navigate the expectations that came with being crowned Prince of the Heavens. The weight of the throne was ever-present, even when he didn’t wear the crown.

Phainon had appeared as he often did, effortlessly entering the space with the quiet chaos that only he seemed capable of causing. The same teasing smirk on his face, the same dangerous allure in his movements, but this time, there was something new in his eyes. A challenge.

Before Mydei could protest, Phainon had dropped down without warning— without any ceremony—right into his lap, draping himself across him like an unruly cat.

“What the hell do you think you’re doing?” Mydei had asked, his voice tight, his face flushed with the suddenness of it. His hands had shot out instinctively to push the incubi away, but Phainon had only laughed, unbothered.

The room had gone silent. There had been whispers, muttered insults from those who thought they could see through this brazen act. “He’s corrupting the Crown Prince,” one had said, their voice thick with disapproval. “A creature like him—this is what comes from consorting with demons.”

Mydei hadn’t noticed the muttering at first. He had been too busy trying to figure out how to get Phainon off his lap, how to contain the unexpected

sensation blooming in his chest. But then the whispers had become louder, more direct. Eyes had turned to him, full of judgment and fear.

He had grown tense, trying to pull away from Phainon, to make some kind of show of it—but Phainon had merely laughed, leaning in closer, his lips brushing Mydei’s ear.

“They don’t know anything about us,” Phainon had whispered, his voice low and dangerous. “But you do.”

That had been the beginning.

Phainon had stayed. And no matter how hard Mydei had tried to pretend it didn’t affect him, something had shifted. And now, here they were.

Back in the present, the room had grown a little warmer, the flickering of lanterns dancing across Mydei’s skin as Phainon shifted on his lap, his body a weight of comfort—something all too familiar. The performance continued around them, but Mydei couldn’t ignore the slight pressure of Phainon’s hands on his legs, his subtle but insistent touch as it moved along his thigh.

“You’ve got no shame,” Mydei murmured, though there was no anger behind the words now. Just a tired resignation.

“I know,” Phainon said, his lips curving into that same damnable smirk. “But you don’t mind.”

Mydei didn’t reply, his body betraying him as he let himself settle back, accepting the warmth and the strange comfort that only Phainon could bring.

It was a game. A dangerous, messy game. But it was their game, and Mydei found that, much to his surprise, he didn’t mind it as much as he used to.

The performance continued to unfold before them, but Mydei’s attention drifted with every subtle shift of Phainon’s body against his. The dancers on

the stage moved in harmony, but all he could focus on was the heat between his legs, the slow, deliberate pressure that Phainon’s body exerted against him. It was an unspoken game—Phainon testing him, pushing boundaries, daring him to feel more, to want more.

At first, it was innocent, or at least Mydei tried to convince himself it was. A languid stretch of Phainon’s hand across his lap, a brush of fingertips over his thigh, which, despite the mildness, sent a jolt of warmth through him. Mydei barely moved, attempting to ignore the gnawing sensation building in his chest, but Phainon’s subtle presence was relentless. His body shifted ever closer, the space between them shrinking with each breath, until Mydei could feel his heartbeat pulsing in time with the slow, lazy drag of Phainon’s hand inching dangerously close to places Mydei wasn’t ready to acknowledge.

“Stop,” Mydei whispered, though the word barely left his lips. It was more an instinct than a command. He couldn’t let himself react too loudly, not in front of everyone. Not when the eyes around them were too busy with the ritual to even notice. But Phainon knew better. He felt every beat of Mydei’s heart, the hesitation that slipped from his tone, and most of all, the tightening in his muscles that gave away more than Mydei would ever admit.

Phainon’s fingers didn’t stop. They didn’t even falter. They moved lower, sliding across Mydei’s skin with an almost unbearable slowness, barely perceptible at first. But that was all Phainon needed—just enough of a touch to keep Mydei’s pulse erratic, his breath shaky. His head tilted just enough that his lips brushed the delicate curve of Mydei’s neck, not soft, but insistent. “You want me to stop?” Phainon’s voice was a low hum, just barely audible, and Mydei’s insides twisted at the sound of it.

Another weak attempt to push him away. “Phainon, stop,” Mydei repeated, but it lacked the force of someone in control. His voice quivered slightly, but the lingering sensation of Phainon’s hand moving lower, the heat of his breath against his ear, made it impossible to fully compose himself.

For a moment, Mydei thought Phainon might pull away, but instead, Phainon pressed closer. His hand continued to trace the line of Mydei’s

waist, the path so slow, so calculated, and so excruciatingly close to the edge that Mydei could feel the last shreds of his composure shattering. Phainon’s head shifted, moving lower, his lips brushing Mydei’s collarbone as though testing for a reaction.

Mydei’s pulse quickened. He couldn’t tell if it was from anger or something else. His breath grew shallow, his chest tight, the burning sensation in his core so vivid he almost couldn’t bear it. But he still fought, still tried to maintain control, even though it was slipping further with every caress.

He opened his mouth to speak again, to push Phainon away properly this time, but the words caught in his throat. Instead, a soft, almost imperceptible moan escaped, a response he couldn’t suppress. It wasn’t the protest Phainon had expected. It was something more vulnerable. Something more like need.

Phainon heard it, and it made his smirk grow wider, though he did nothing more than lean into the touch, allowing the moment to linger longer than Mydei could handle. His hand reached lower still, brushing over the waistband of Mydei’s trousers. Every muscle in Mydei’s body tensed, and for just a heartbeat, he thought he might explode from the sheer tension. His breath was ragged, and for a moment, he thought he might lose himself to the heat of Phainon’s touch.

And then, just as suddenly as it began, Phainon stopped.

Mydei’s breath hitched, the sudden halt leaving him strangely empty, like something had been ripped away before he could come to terms with it. Phainon’s hand stilled, and for a long, pregnant moment, neither of them spoke.

Phainon, his face buried in the crook of Mydei’s neck, let out a soft sigh, something between regret and something darker—something more selfish. “I… went too far,” he murmured, though there was no apology in his tone. It was a statement. A fact. He was still so close that Mydei could feel the warmth of his body, the heat radiating from him. And though Phainon had stopped, the tension in the air thickened instead of dissipating.

Mydei’s heart was still racing, and it wasn’t just from the discomfort of being so exposed. There was a lingering sensation of hunger that he couldn’t shake, a heat that clung to his skin and curled under his ribs. Despite himself, he found himself wanting more—his body betraying him.

He swallowed hard, finally breaking the silence. “Don’t… don’t do that again,” Mydei said, though his voice was almost strained, like he wasn’t sure he meant it. His words should have sounded firm, but instead they came out shaky, barely able to mask the burning desire that hadn’t gone away.

Phainon didn’t respond at first. Instead, he pressed his face further into Mydei’s neck, his lips brushing lightly against the skin. “I won’t,” he said quietly, though the edge in his voice made it clear he didn’t truly mean it. Not in the way Mydei would have liked.

The air between them was electric, filled with a tension so thick it was suffocating. Mydei’s thoughts were tangled, and even though Phainon had pulled away physically, it was impossible to shake the grip he still had on him—on his body, on his emotions, on everything.

It was maddening.

He indulged it anyway.
