The moon loomed high, swollen with silver light, casting its glow over the endless stretch of the heavens. Phainon stood at the edge of an otherworldly precipice, the ground beneath him smooth as polished bone, dissolving into mist where it met the void. A place untouched, unmarred, where the unworthy could not tread.

Below, the Sanctum of Aetherion shimmered—a temple carved from veined gold and lapis, its spires piercing the fabric of the cosmos itself. It hovered in stillness, defying gravity, a place where only the highest of celestial beings were permitted entry. A sacred ground. A realm of gods.

And Phainon could go no further.

His eyes remained locked on the distant structure, expression unreadable. He did not pace, did not shift—he simply waited. His usual languid ease

was absent, tension coiled beneath his skin like a beast restrained.

The hunger clawed at him.

Not for the temple itself—he had no interest in begging for a seat at a table that would never welcome him. The heavens had long tolerated his existence, nothing more. That was a battle he’d stopped fighting ages ago.

But Mydei was in there.

And that was the real test.

The celestial alignment had begun a month ago. A rare event, one that came only once every few centuries, when the stars shifted in their grand design and the very air became thick with purity.

Aetheris, the Month of Ascension.

For gods, it was a time of renewal. For incubi, it was a curse.

Phainon had gone thirty days without feeding. No indulgence, no stolen pleasure, nothing to sate the gnawing void in his chest. He told himself it was a game—a test of his own willpower, a way to amuse himself.

But that was a lie.

It was never just a game. He was proving something.

That he could endure. That he could be more than his nature. That he could stand at Mydei’s side as an equal, not a creature bound by base instincts.

Yet even now, his restraint was slipping.

He could feel Mydei’s presence, a storm of power radiating from within those gilded halls, amplified a thousandfold by the rites taking place inside. It wasn’t just strength—it was a pull, something ancient and unrelenting, something Phainon felt in the marrow of his being.

His fingers curled into fists.

The sheer force of Mydei’s energy, heightened by the rites of Aetheris, was overwhelming. Phainon could taste it in the air, the weight of it pressing against his skin like an unspoken challenge. It was unbearable.

His body screamed at him to take, to consume, to devour.

He exhaled sharply, forcing his muscles to loosen, shoving the hunger back down where it belonged.

Not yet. Not like this.

He would not crawl. He would not beg.

He would endure.

If he could make it through this night—just one more night—he would have proven himself.

And when Mydei finally emerged from that sanctum, glowing with the aftermath of whatever holy rites had transpired inside, Phainon would meet him with a smirk, as if none of this had touched him at all.

Even if it destroyed him.

Phainon remained where he was, perched at the cliff’s edge like a creature of ruin staring into a world that did not want him. The temple’s golden gates finally parted, a soft, resonant hum filling the space as figures emerged, bathed in the ethereal light of Aetheris.

And there he was.

Mydei stepped into the open air, his presence a force unto itself. The celestial rites still clung to him, settling into his skin like stardust, woven into the folds of his robes. His posture was straight, every movement controlled, effortless. The sheer weight of his divinity was staggering.

But it wasn’t just his power.

It was the sharp cut of his jaw, the unwavering set of his gaze, the way his presence commanded the space around him without a word. He looked untouchable. Unshaken. Regal.

Phainon’s lips curled slightly, lazy amusement flickering in his gaze. It was always a sight to behold—this Mydei.

Yet his attention soon drifted to the figure walking beside him.

A Damion.

That was the closest approximation to what they were called, though there was no true translation in human tongues. A being forged from light, neither mortal nor god, bound to the will of the heavens. They were guardians, messengers, watchers—a class of celestial beings just beneath the gods themselves.

And this one walked beside Mydei as if they were equals.

Phainon tilted his head slightly, watching them converse. The Damion’s tone was respectful, but something in the cadence of their voice was just a fraction too careful, too measured.

They did not look at Mydei as one looks at a prince, but rather as one looks at something sacred, something untouchable.

Phainon had seen that kind of reverence before. It was a reverence that demanded distance.

He remained where he was, an idle observer, fingers tapping against his knee in slow, rhythmic beats. He didn’t move, didn’t speak—he simply watched.

And then, the Damion’s gaze flickered toward him.

They did not react outright. There was no sneer, no open disdain. Their face remained impassive, expression crafted with careful neutrality, but something in their bearing shifted, almost imperceptibly. A stiffness in the shoulders. A quiet tension.

Like a blade being restrained from being drawn.

They did not speak to him. They wouldn’t dare.

Not because of what he was. Because of who he belonged to.

Phainon hummed under his breath, eyes half-lidded, feigning disinterest even as the moment stretched. This was nothing new.

Tolerated. Never accepted.

The amusement should have been bitter.

Instead, it vanished entirely the moment Mydei’s gaze landed on him.

Without hesitation, without a second thought, the Crown Prince turned away from the Damion and strode toward him. The dismissal was not cruel, not unkind—but it was final.

And Phainon, despite himself, felt his lips twitch upward.

Just slightly.

Not enough to be a smirk, not enough to betray anything—but enough to take note of the near-imperceptible shift in Damion’s expression.

There was no anger. No disrespect. Only the slightest tightening of their jaw, the briefest flicker in their expression before it was smoothed away.

Because for all their divine status, for all the ceremony and reverence that surrounded them—

They had just been dismissed in favor of an incubi.

And they could do nothing about it.

Phainon didn’t bother standing. He remained seated at the cliff’s edge, head tilted just slightly, watching Mydei approach with that ever-present languid ease. The prince looked as composed as ever, but Phainon didn’t miss the

way his gaze flickered—subtle, assessing, like he was already preparing for whatever nonsense the incubi was about to pull.

“You know,” Phainon drawled, stretching his arms behind his head, “I almost thought you wouldn’t notice me.”

Mydei stopped a few paces away, giving him a look that was somewhere between exasperation and amusement. “I always notice you. That’s the problem.”

Phainon grinned. “Flattering.”

“It wasn’t meant to be.”

Mydei turned slightly, already moving past him as if to leave this exchange at that, but Phainon, of course, had other plans.

With a deliberate motion, he unfurled his tail.

It wasn’t often that he used it so openly. The sleek, dark appendage— normally coiled around his waist or kept out of sight—moved with ease, curving through the air before wrapping gently around Mydei’s forearm.

And then, without a word, Phainon pulled.

It wasn’t rough, wasn’t forceful—just a slow, insistent tug meant to guide rather than drag. A silent, move it along.

Mydei let out a short, irritated-sounding exhale, but he didn’t resist. Didn’t even try.

He just grumbled under his breath and kept walking.

Phainon’s tail remained looped around him, a loose tether.

From the corner of his eye, Phainon caught the movement.

Damion took a step forward. A small one. Barely noticeable, but there. Their posture shifted, their weight subtly redistributed—a telltale sign of

someone suppressing the instinct to intervene.

Because to them, this was irreverence. This was audacity.

An incubi, touching the Crown Prince so casually? Handling him as if they were equals? Unthinkable.

But before Damion could act—before they could so much as open their mouth—Mydei shot them a glance.

Not sharp. Not reprimanding. Just a look.

A simple, wordless confirmation that he had no issue with this. That there was no need for intervention.

That he didn’t care.

And Damion, despite their station, despite everything, had no choice but to accept that.

Phainon felt the corner of his mouth twitch upward once again.

Oh, he had noticed that.

Phainon let himself fall into step beside him, gaze drifting idly as they moved. The Damion was gone now, but their presence lingered, like a song cut off before the final note.

Phainon’s tail loosened slightly from Mydei’s arm but didn’t retreat entirely, the tip flicking lazily against the fabric of his sleeve. It wasn’t intentional. Or maybe it was. He wasn’t in the mood to think too deeply about it.

They walked in silence for a while, the path before them smooth and untouched. Then, without warning, Mydei veered. A shift so subtle that most wouldn’t have caught it, but Phainon wasn’t most. His steps faltered for half a second before he adjusted, his tail curling instinctively tighter as if to reel Mydei back in.

Instead, he let himself be guided.

Still, his hand lifted, fingers catching Mydei’s wrist—not to stop him, not even to question. Just to feel the pulse beneath his skin, the warmth.

“Mm?” Phainon’s hum was low, inquisitive. Not pressing, not demanding. Just a soft sound of acknowledgment.

Mydei didn’t answer immediately. His face remained impassive, unreadable, but for a single breath, something shifted. It wasn’t much—just a flicker, an unreadable something behind his eyes—but Phainon caught it.

And then, just as quickly, it was gone.

Phainon tilted his head slightly, but the smile he conjured was effortless. “Going somewhere?”

Mydei’s gaze flicked to him, unreadable still. “Does it matter?”

Phainon let out a quiet chuckle, releasing his wrist as he stepped closer, their arms brushing. “Not at all.”

His tail uncurled fully this time, slipping away. But still, it hovered, close enough that the warmth remained.

They continued forward, side by side, and Phainon told himself it meant nothing.

But he had seen that flicker.

And he wanted to know what it meant.

As they walked, the air between them was quiet—not heavy, not tense. Just quiet. A rare sort of stillness that Phainon wasn’t entirely used to, but didn’t mind.

Then, soft and low, Mydei began to hum.

It was simple, unembellished—not meant for an audience, not meant for anyone at all. Just something effortless, something that settled into the space between them without needing to be acknowledged.

And Phainon, without thinking, listened.

His gaze stayed forward, but his steps synced unconsciously with the rhythm. He didn’t recognize the melody, didn’t know if it was something old or something Mydei had merely strung together absentmindedly.

It didn’t matter.

What did matter was the sudden, firm grasp around his wrist.

Phainon blinked as Mydei’s fingers wrapped around him—not harsh, not hurried, but with a certainty that didn’t allow for argument. Then, without a word, Mydei changed direction again, dragging him along.

Phainon let himself be led, more curious than anything. He could have resisted if he wanted to, but he didn’t. Instead, he followed, steps loose and easy as Mydei pulled him toward what looked like… nothing.

Just empty space.

Blank, untouched, unremarkable. Nothingness stretched out before them, seamless and endless, and yet Mydei didn’t pause. Didn’t hesitate.

Phainon arched a brow, lips curving slightly. “Fascinating,” he mused. “You’ve brought me to absolutely nowhere.”

Mydei didn’t respond, too focused on… something.

He shifted slightly, adjusting his stance, gaze sharp as if aligning himself with an unseen mark. Then, with a final movement—one that felt deliberate, purposeful—he stepped forward.

And the nothingness peeled away.

Like a veil being lifted, reality seemed to bend, unfold, reshape. Structures materialized where there had been none, shelves stretching high and endless, gilded spines catching the light of unseen flames. The scent of parchment and ink drifted through the air, mingling with something older, something deeper—the weight of knowledge itself.

A library.

Phainon let out a low breath, his amusement shifting into something genuine, intrigued.

Mydei finally released him, gesturing toward the expanse before them. “Welcome,” he said smoothly, “to my library.”

Phainon took a slow step forward, gaze flickering over the towering shelves, the countless tomes. Then, lazily, he turned to Mydei, expression unreadable.

“You can read?”

Mydei blinked once, slow.

Then, ever so slightly, his brows knit together, an almost imperceptible shift —like he wasn’t sure whether to be offended or amused.

“…Brat,” he muttered, exhaling through his nose.

Then, without another word, he turned his back on Phainon and strode forward, stepping deeper into the library. His presence fit the space too well —like he belonged here, like this place had been shaped around him rather than the other way around.

“Read. Don’t read,” Mydei said idly over his shoulder. “Just don’t touch anything you shouldn’t.”

Phainon grinned, watching him go, sharp and entertained. Now that was interesting.

Phainon stretched languidly, arms arching over his head, tail flicking in idle amusement as he leaned just a little too far back—

A soft thud sounded as his hand barely grazed the edge of a precariously stacked tome.

Mydei, without even turning around, let out a warning sigh.

Phainon huffed a quiet laugh but straightened, lazily scanning the shelves. The library was vast, lined with books of every size, their spines worn with age or pristine in their bindings. He wasn’t much for reading—not like Mydei, who had that unfairly sharp mind and the patience for all this.

But then—something caught his eye.

A book, tucked neatly among the rest, its title etched in a script that wasn’t just old. It was ancient.

Phainon’s fingers paused above the spine. His eyes narrowed slightly.

Kremnoan.

A language almost forgotten, its words older than empires, forged in a place that most considered half myth, half grave.

Castrum Kremnos.

Phainon knew of it—not just from records, but from Mydei himself. From the rare, fleeting moments when the prince let something slip.

Like when Phainon had grinned at him, sharp and teasing, and drawled, What, are you scared?

And Mydei, without missing a beat, had said, Kremnos has no word for fear.

Or when Phainon, ever the instigator, had pushed further teasing, No word for giving up, either? Or surrender? Or regret?

And Mydei, ever the same, had simply replied, No.

Phainon had laughed, shaking his head. I’m starting to wonder if your language has any words at all.

And Mydei had only looked at him, silent, unreadable.

Phainon ran a finger along the spine of the book.

Well. Time to find out.

With a quiet hum, he pulled it from the shelf.

Phainon had lost track of time.

He had settled into a quiet corner of the library, a space that felt untouched, almost forgotten. The chair beneath him was far too comfortable, and the book in his hands, though heavy, sat easily in his grasp.

At first, he had only skimmed, expecting dense, rigid text. But the deeper he read, the more the words pulled him in.

The language was old, unfamiliar—its rhythm unlike anything he knew. And yet, something about it felt close. Like hearing the echo of a song he didn’t remember learning.

His gaze flickered up for just a moment. Across the room, Mydei sat deep in thought, completely still, as if the rest of the world had never touched him. He always looked that way—untouched, unmoved, set apart in a way that seemed almost effortless.

Phainon’s fingers drifted over the page before he turned it.

Then, he stopped.

A single word stood out.

EKTHA.

His brow furrowed slightly. Without thinking, he ran his fingers over the ink, tracing the letters in silence.

Unchanging oath. A bond that cannot be severed.

The meaning lingered in his thoughts, settling into a space he hadn’t realized was open.

A bond that couldn’t be severed.

Phainon exhaled slowly, tilting his head back. It was an odd thing, for a language to have such certainty in a single word. To define something so absolute, without hesitation.

A promise that didn’t break. A tie that didn’t fray.

He let the thought drift for a while, rolling it over in his mind. Then, with a quiet chuckle—more amused than anything—he shook his head and turned the page.

The sound of a book snapping shut broke the silence.

“We should go.”

Phainon blinked, dragging himself back to the present.

Mydei stood beside him, as calm as ever, though his gaze flickered—just briefly—to the book in Phainon’s hands.

Without waiting for an answer, he sat down, his movement unhurried. He leaned in slightly, eyes skimming over the text.

Phainon didn’t move, though he was keenly aware of the shift in space, of Mydei’s presence now close.

“What is it?” Mydei asked, voice quiet.

Phainon hesitated, then tilted the book just enough for him to see. “Something I found.”

His gaze lingered on EKTHA.

Mydei didn’t comment, but his attention stayed on the page. If he noticed the significance, he didn’t say.

“You got quiet,” he mused instead, his tone light. “Didn’t think you’d get caught up in a book.”

Phainon smirked lazily. “Guess I found something interesting.”

Mydei huffed a soft laugh, his lips curving faintly. “You always do.”

Then, without warning, he took the book from Phainon’s hands and stood.

“Let’s go,” he said again, tone casual but not leaving room for argument. “No need to sit here all night.”

Phainon sighed, rolling his shoulders as he got to his feet, his tail flicking lazily behind him. “You really don’t have patience, do you?”

Mydei was already walking, not bothering to answer.

Phainon shook his head, falling into step beside him.

For a while, neither of them spoke. The silence was comfortable, stretching between them like an old habit.

Then, just as Phainon was slipping back into his thoughts, Mydei exhaled— a quiet, almost absent sound.

“I’ll bring you next time too.”

Phainon didn’t react right away, but something in him settled, just a little.

It wasn’t a grand gesture. Not a promise, not a declaration.

But it was something.

And somehow, that was enough.

A slow smile tugged at Phainon’s lips as he adjusted his pace, falling into stride with Mydei.

Next time.

Maybe that wasn’t so bad.

Phainon sprawled across the ground, arms stretched lazily over the cool stone, eyes fixed on the sky. The sun hung high, golden light pouring down in soft waves. A perfect afternoon.

And yet, here he was—stuck outside. Again.

They had arrived at Thalorionis, the underground sanctuary buried beneath the citadel. A place steeped in importance, where names carried weight and decisions shaped the future. But as always, politics had shut him out. Meetings, negotiations, alliances—things that, according to everyone else, had nothing to do with him.

So he waited. Alone. Watching the sky, listening to the distant hum of the world moving without him.

Phainon sighed and turned his head, trying to find something remotely interesting in the view. But there was only stone, shadows stretching with the slow turn of the sun, and the massive, ancient entrance of Thalorionis looming in the distance.

After a few moments of staring into the light, his eyes started to sting. He blinked rapidly, rubbing at them with the back of his hand.

“Damn,” he muttered. “Guess that’s what I get for trying to have a staring contest with the sun.”

With a grunt, he sat up, brushing the dust from his clothes. The feeling that had followed him since they arrived—something between boredom and frustration—hadn’t faded. If anything, it had settled deeper.

He let himself flop back down with a sigh, not to sleep, just to be. The faint breeze curled around him, carrying distant echoes of movement from within Thalorionis. There was an odd comfort to it, the quiet, the steady pulse of life beneath the surface.

His thoughts drifted.

“Thalorionis,” he murmured, his voice barely above a breath, “stretches for miles underground… practically its own world down there. Entire cities, buried under stone. Like a labyrinth.”

He exhaled slowly, staring up at the sky as his mind wandered.

“Some levels are so old, no one even knows what they were built for… they say there are entire districts that have been sealed off for centuries…”

The words came lazily, unraveling in half-formed thoughts. He wasn’t even sure who he was talking to—maybe just himself, maybe the air, maybe no one at all.

“…Would be nice to see it.”

The thought landed heavier than he expected.

His fingers twitched. His tail flicked once against the ground.

He sat up abruptly.

His gaze locked onto the entrance—ancient stone carved with symbols older than most living memory. Mydei was in there, along with all the others. The ones who belonged there. The ones making decisions, shaping outcomes, moving forward while he sat outside, waiting for permission that would never come.

Phainon clicked his tongue, irritation sparking at the edges of his thoughts.

It wasn’t just curiosity. It wasn’t just boredom.

He wanted in.

He stood, brushing himself off, eyes narrowing as he studied the entrance.

“Maybe just a quick look,” he muttered to himself, licking his lips. A stupid thought, really. But the more he let it sit, the more it felt like the only logical thing to do.

He wasn’t content to sit and wait.

Not today.

Phainon ran a hand through his hair, exhaling slowly as he eyed the entrance to Thalorionis. The structure loomed before him, ancient and unwavering, the stonework etched with markings older than most civilizations. No guards, no patrols. Just two massive sentinels carved from obsidian and veined with something that pulsed faintly beneath the surface.

He recognized them immediately. Astrothes. The Unyielding Witnesses.

Legends claimed they had been shaped by the first architects of Thalorionis, their purpose singular—to judge. Not by choice, not by bias, but by an unwavering, incorruptible truth. Their gaze could strip away all deception, reducing the unworthy to nothing more than dust on the threshold.

And he was very much unworthy.

Phainon clicked his tongue, folding his arms as he studied them. Their eyes —deep, faceted crystal set into their unmoving faces—glowed faintly, a silent reminder that purity was the only currency accepted here.

Which meant he needed to cheat.

He wasn’t the only one unable to enter. Thalorionis wasn’t just a sacred ground; it was submerged in anatevrian waters, the kind that recognized only the unstained. The devout, the righteous. Unfortunately, that list didn’t include him.

But it also didn’t include a good number of others—envoys, scribes, lesser nobility. And for them, there were relics.

Phainon’s lips curled into a slow smirk. That’ll do.

Now, he just had to find one.

He stepped away from the entrance, scanning the gathering outside. Not everyone had been granted immediate access. There were always people

lingering—some waiting, some whispering amongst themselves, some clearly frustrated by the restrictions.

And then he spotted his mark.

A younger man, robed in deep blue, fingers curled tightly around a small pendant at his throat. Nervous, pacing, muttering under his breath. The way he kept glancing toward the entrance and adjusting the chain around his neck told Phainon everything he needed to know.

That’s it.

He straightened, slipping into a more composed stance, expression smoothing into something gentler, more refined. He didn’t look like an incubi. Snow-white hair, blue eyes—if anything, he carried the features of something closer to an angel, if not for the way he usually carried himself. But now, he could make use of it.

Adopting an air of quiet grace, he approached, careful to move with a presence that suggested authority without outright demanding it. The young man barely noticed him at first, too caught up in his own frustrations.

Phainon tilted his head, voice calm, almost sympathetic. “Trouble getting in?”

The man startled slightly, looking up. “Ah—yes. I—” He hesitated, then exhaled sharply. “The Astrothes haven’t acknowledged my entrance yet.”

Phainon’s gaze flicked briefly to the relic at the man’s throat before returning to his face. “Unfortunate.”

The man huffed, clearly distressed. “I was assured this would work. My family has long held ties with Thalorionis—there shouldn’t be any issue.”

Phainon offered a slow nod, as if in understanding. Then, with just the right amount of curiosity, he asked, “May I?”

The man blinked, confused. “May you…?”

Phainon gestured subtly to the relic. “Your pendant. If it’s meant to grant passage, there may be a way to reinforce its presence. Sometimes the anatevrian waters resist weak blessings. I’ve seen it before.”

A blatant lie, but he delivered it with such quiet confidence that the man hesitated only a moment before nodding and undoing the clasp.

The second it was in Phainon’s hands, he acted.

A brief shift of fingers, a subtle flick of movement—and the pendant was his.

He returned a different chain, similar enough in weight and feel that the man wouldn’t immediately notice. Then, with a reassuring smile, Phainon placed a hand on his shoulder. “Give it a moment. The Astrothes will recognize it soon.”

The man looked relieved, nodding quickly as he stepped toward the entrance once more.

Phainon turned before he could see the deception unravel.

With the stolen relic now safely in his grasp, he moved toward the threshold, slipping the pendant over his head. The cool metal rested against his skin, a faint hum resonating through it.

This was it.

Taking a breath, he stepped forward.

The Astrothes remained still, their crystal eyes locking onto him. For a split second, a terrible silence filled the space between them, the pressure of judgment creeping in.

Phainon didn’t falter. He kept his pace steady, his expression neutral.

Then—

The glow in their eyes dimmed.

They did not move. They did not reject him.

The relic had done its job.

Phainon stepped past them, feeling the shift in the air, the sensation of crossing from one world into another.

And just like that—

He was in.

Phainon stepped through the threshold, and the world changed.

Light bent around him, impossibly bright, filtered through sapphire waters. What lay beyond the gates of Thalorionis wasn’t a city—it was a legend, alive and breathing. Great coral palaces stretched high into the depths, their spiraling towers woven from living reef and stone, crowned with glass domes that shimmered like trapped stars. Sanctuaries floated between them, suspended by thin currents of light, tethered only by strands of woven kelp and ancient incantations.

The streets glittered beneath his feet, paved in crushed pearl and tempered glass. Above, aqueducts of crystalline water arched through the open spaces, carrying shimmering schools of fish and streaks of bioluminescent flora. The very air hummed, thick with old seals and protective rites meant to keep things like him out—a persistent pressure against his skin, like a thousand hands trying to push him away.

If not for the relic hanging loosely around his neck, he was certain he’d be a smear on the polished stones by now.

He took a breath—sharp, cold, too clean. It didn’t taste like air. It tasted like something long untouched by corruption or grief, and it made his stomach twist in a way he didn’t care to dwell on.

Gods, it was beautiful.

Phainon let out a slow whistle, running a hand through his pale hair as his gaze tracked the layers of life moving through the place. Purveyor’s balanced trays of glimmering offerings, robed figures spoke in lilting chants, and statues too perfect to be mortal lined every street corner, their expressions caught forever between sorrow and joy.

A place like this shouldn’t exist.

And yet here it was—and here he was, standing in its heart like he belonged.

“Well,” Phainon muttered to no one in particular, a crooked grin tugging at his lips. “Guess they’ll let anyone in these days.”

The pulse of wards and spells prickled at his skin as he moved deeper into the city, but the relic did its work. The pressure faded to a dull thrum at the base of his skull, leaving only awe in its wake. He didn’t even try to hide it —the wide eyes, the way his head tilted to track the ghostly glow of a sea serpent as it wound lazily past a temple spire.

It was a miracle.

And for once, Phainon wasn’t in a rush to ruin it.

Phainon stretched his arms over his head, rolling the tension from his shoulders as he took in the impossible sprawl of Thalorionis. No wonder the old texts spoke of it like a lost Eden. The entire city moved like a living thing—coral towers shifting with the slow pulse of the deep, bridges of translucent stone breathing faintly beneath his feet, and great sanctums

suspended by chains of woven starlight, drifting in the currents like sunken moons.

There were no merchants hawking wares or common stalls cluttering the streets like in the mortal world. Here, trade happened through unspoken gestures and exchanges of essence. Glass reliquaries hung between archways, each containing fragments of light, strands of woven memory, or shimmering beads of condensed song. Offerings passed hands without a word. It wasn’t about price, though.

The economy of Thalorionis, as it turned out, was built on blood—both figuratively and otherwise. The pure-blooded, those descended from celestial lines or born beneath the veil of the Titans, possessed an innate right to claim whatever they desired. Their virtue alone was considered currency, their very presence a tithe to the city’s hallowed grounds. The sanctified scrolls called it Anaktora Dorea, the Gift of Sovereigns—the belief that those born flawless were the living embodiment of providence itself, and to deny them was to deny the natural order.

For everyone else?

A drop of blood.

A sacred cut at the wrist or fingertip, given freely into consecrated vessels. It wasn’t payment, not by their standards—it was offering. A blessing in disguise. The vitae shed was said to bind the supplicant closer to the divine waters, cleansing mortal fault and making one known to the city itself. So the priests claimed.

To Phainon, it was mostly inconvenient.

He absently palmed one of the slim coins hidden in his sleeve, the metal cool against his skin. Relics like the one around his neck could bypass most of the formalities, their blessings ancient enough to permit material currency. Technically. It wasn’t exactly illegal. Just… distasteful. A stranger using forged blessings and weightless gold in a place where even a whisper of corruption could sour the water.

Not that it stopped him.

When no one was looking, he slipped a coin into a floating basin cradled by a figure of bleached stone, snagged a cluster of sun-dried lotus petals dusted with stardust resin, and popped one into his mouth with a sharp grin.

Sweet. Crisp. Nothing like surface food. Every bite felt radiant, like eating preserved light.

He took his time wandering through the towering halls and delicate causeways, watching as plumes of bioluminescent mist curled from the mouths of carved leviathans, and streams of mirrored fish spun like threads through the open domes. Somewhere above, a choir of unseen voices sang a wordless hymn, and for a moment, the city felt less like a place and more like a dream someone had forgotten to wake from.

Phainon tilted his head back, letting the glow of the sun through the water bathe his face, and smiled to himself.

“Well,” he muttered under his breath, “could be worse.”

And with that, he moved deeper into Thalorionis, eager to see what else the so-called paradise had to offer before someone figured out he had no business being there.

Phainon didn’t mean to start devouring everything in sight—it just kind of happened.

It began innocently enough: a passing tray of something that looked like spun glass, delicate threads of iridescent silk coiled into the shape of a blossom. He didn’t even ask what it was. Just snatched one up when no one was looking and bit in. It dissolved on his tongue like frost, leaving behind the taste of honeyed sea-salt and something almost floral, something that made the back of his throat tingle.

From there, it spiraled.

He wandered between open sanctums and vaulted galleries, snagging whatever looked edible—shimmering fruits that bled liquid starlight when bitten into, tiny spheres of chilled nectar that floated in the air until you caught them with your teeth, roasted petals glazed in thick, sun-golden syrup.

At one point, he passed a vessel made of crystal coral, inside which lay what appeared to be a single, perfect oyster, its shell lined in opal. A passing attendant in a trailing, pale robe gave him a bemused glance when he reached for it, but made no move to stop him.

Phainon grinned and knocked it back like a shot.

Mistake.

The texture was all wrong. Like drinking liquid velvet while chewing on something that might have once been a flower. The taste? Sharp and freezing, then cloyingly sweet, like biting through frost into molten honey. His eyes watered. His stomach lurched. He swallowed it anyway.

“Alright,” he rasped, voice rough, “probably not for surface dwellers.”

A few of the pure-blooded onlookers—dressed in whisper-thin silk and draped in relic-threaded jewels—watched him with polite wariness, a few arching pale brows when he flicked another coin into a basin to pay for a piece of what looked like glazed tidefruit. Phainon could practically feel their judgment, subtle and cold like mist against his skin.

No one said a word, though. Which was a marked improvement compared to the usual jeering contempt he got back home, where every side-eye and muttered remark around the Council chambers came with a reminder that he was either a charity case, a mistake, or worse.

Here, at least, no one knew his name. They just thought he was an odd angel with bad table manners.

He could live with that.

By the time he reached a massive, tiered fountain where glowing syrup cascaded down like molten glass, Phainon’s stomach ached in a way it hadn’t in years. None of this was real sustenance for him—not the kind his body craved. But gods, it tasted good. And after a while, that was enough.

He snatched a skewer of something blistered and glazed from a passing silver dish—some kind of sea-creature, charred until the flesh crackled under his teeth and smoked when he bit in—and grunted in approval.

A few nearby purebloods shot him scandalized looks at the sheer feralness of his eating habits, one murmuring something in a liquid, ancient tongue that Phainon didn’t bother deciphering. He winked at them, wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, and grabbed another.

Maybe he’d die from one of these things. Maybe not.

Either way, he was eating good tonight.

Phainon was elbow-deep in something that probably wasn’t meant to be eaten by creatures born of shadow and spite, but at this point, he’d given up trying to figure out what half the shimmering dishes even were. The food here was impossible—petal-thin wafers that dissolved into warmth and light on his tongue, spiced broths that shimmered with constellations, fruits that bled silver nectar. He didn’t care what any of it was. He was starving, and the taste was unreal.

The configurer, a tall figure whose face flickered like water catching light, shot him a suspicious glance as he slipped a few coins onto the offering dish. The act earned a faint sniff of disdain, but no words. Fine by him. At least no one here was throwing him through a wall or hissing about him sullying their sacred halls.

He reached for something that looked like a skewer of candied storm pearls when a tiny hand suddenly tugged at the edge of his sleeve.

Phainon blinked down.

A child. Or… something like one. Its skin shimmered opalescent, eyes wide and the color of dawn breaking over the sea. An Archon fledgling, judging by the faint flicker of sigils hovering around its brow. No older than seven or eight by human standards—which meant probably older than him, in some twisted cosmic sense.

The kid just stared at him, expression solemn and awed.

“Are you…” the child whispered, voice soft as ripples on glass. “One of the Choir?”

Phainon choked slightly on a bite of something unnervingly delicious. “Me? Uh—yeah. Totally. One of those. Choir boy, through and through.” He grinned, a little too sharp.

The child brightened, clapping tiny hands together in glee. “Mama says when the Aetheris light touches down, the Choir sends one to watch over us.”

Before he could stop it—or object, or run—the kid raised a hand, delicate fingers glowing with the warm, iridescent shimmer of a benediction.

“By the Veiled Crown and Light of the Starborn Depths, I offer you grace.”

Oh, shit.

A sharp, warm jolt struck him in the chest. It wasn’t like flame—no, this was clean. Light without shadow,  so bright it made his stomach knot. For a split second, his skin prickled and his breath hitched—relic working overtime, the buffer between his cursed nature and divine power barely holding.

And then it was over.

The kid smiled, patted his hand, and skipped off like nothing had happened.

Phainon stood frozen for a beat, pulse hammering. He exhaled slowly, muttering under his breath, “That… could’ve been worse.”

He turned—and immediately noticed several nearby purebloods and retainers watching him with mild reverence. A few even inclined their heads. One of the older ones murmured something about “Celestine favor.”

Phainon gave them his most beatific, holier-than-thou smile. “Blessings upon you all,” he purred, then promptly bolted down the next street before anyone could get a better look.

Phainon rounded the corner, ducking beneath the arch of a half-crumbling coral overpass and weaving into a narrow, dim-lit alcove tucked between two shrines slick with bioluminescent moss. Only when he was out of sight did he let the holy grin drop off his face like a mask snapping loose.

He dropped to his knees in a harsh thud, a ragged gasp tearing from his throat.

Fuck.

It hit him all at once—the air, the residual blessing clinging to his skin like frostbite, the searing ache in his chest. His head tipped back against the cool stone, throat working as he sucked in air that felt like knives.

What the hell was he doing?

Sneaking into Thalorionis during the Month of Aetheris? Getting blessed by some fledgling Archon? Smiling at purebloods like he belonged here?

He barked out a hoarse, humorless laugh that immediately choked off into a groan as another pang tore through his stomach—not hunger for food, but something worse. An ache gnawing at the marrow of him.

It wasn’t like he hadn’t felt it before—every year when the stars aligned and the holy light of Aetheris drowned the skies and seas, incubi and their kind crawled into whatever shadows they could find to wait it out. The Month of Aetheris wasn’t for them. It was for renewal, for blessing, for the God’s bloodline.

And for people like him, it was a curse.

He’d been holding out for weeks, avoiding the itch, the hollow pit in his gut that no food or light could fill. And now—surrounded by pureblood familiars, holy air thick as syrup, divine seals woven into every crack of the city—it came rushing in like a wave, crashing down and dragging him under.

He gritted his teeth, shoving a hand through his hair. It stuck to his forehead, damp with cold sweat.

“Okay, okay, you’re fine,” he muttered. “This is fine. This is… fine adjacent.”

His stomach twisted again, and he curled in on himself briefly, pressing his palm flat to the stone floor, letting the cool bite of it anchor him.

I should leave. I should get the fuck out.

Except he couldn’t. Not yet. Not without drawing attention. Not with the city guards still prowling the upper levels and those damn stone wardens at the exits.

And not while his relic’s buffer was still holding.

He took a breath, slower this time. The ache didn’t ease, but it dulled to something manageable—barely.

“Alright,” he rasped to the empty alley, dragging himself to his feet with a grimace. “One more loop around. No weird holy kids. No more free blessings. No duels. Just… keep your head down, dumbass.”

It wasn’t the best plan.

But he’d made worse.

Phainon forced himself upright.

It wasn’t graceful. His limbs felt too long, his skin too tight, a pulse beneath it that didn’t belong to him. The polished stone walls shimmered faintly around him, halos of light bending and twitching at the edges of his vision.

His reflection in a water-veiled archway caught his eye—pale skin a little too bloodless now, those sharp blue eyes clouded with something inky swimming just beneath the surface. His lips quirked in a bitter grin. He looked like a ghost, or worse, one of them.

Rein it in. Pull yourself together.

Phainon swallowed hard, ignoring the way his throat felt raw as he straightened his shoulders and set one foot ahead of the other. Each step felt jagged, his bones scraping together like ill-fitted clockwork, but he moved. He could pretend. He always could.

Walk. Think. Find a way out.

Astrothes still stood at the city’s front—those stone monstrosities weren’t moving for anyone. And his relic’s trick wouldn’t hold long if anyone else got too curious.

His path took him through an open courtyard, the kind built for no reason other than to humble lesser beings. Enormous coral pillars wreathed in bioluminescent vines reached up to the domed ceiling above, and a soft, shimmering mist hung in the air like some sacred veil.

He should’ve kept walking.

But his feet stopped.

He heard it before he truly saw it—the low hum of energy, the sharp clash of steel, and the unearthly thrumm of sigils flaring mid-air.

A Duel of Aetheris.

Shit.

Even in a place like this, it was rare to see one up close. The Month of Aetheris wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows—it was tradition. Gods and their highest familiars clashed in ritual combat, offerings of strength, light, and loyalty spilled across consecrated grounds.

It took him a second to realize what he was actually looking at.

These weren’t mortals.

They weren’t even lesser divine.

No—the way the air around them crackled, how the ground itself shimmered at their feet, marked them for what they were.

High familiars.

Born from the rivers of fate. From the breath of storm titans. From light made manifest.

Phainon’s stomach twisted viciously.

The ache wasn’t dull anymore. It gnawed at him, curling cold fingers up his spine and latching onto the base of his skull. His vision hazed, edges of the world blurring and warping in sickly hues. He could smell it—the sanctity radiating off them in waves, a sickly-sweet thing that made his head swim.

His kind wasn’t meant to be here. His blood didn’t belong in this light.

And his own nature, that deep, crawling hunger, was waking up.

He pressed a palm hard to his chest, felt the thrum of his pulse—too fast, too sharp.

“Keep moving…” he hissed under his breath, forcing his legs to take a step. Then another. Each one a battle in itself.

But against his better judgment, his eyes were still locked on the dueling grounds. The sigils, the elegance of the fight, the raw power. It was intoxicating in the worst way.

And somewhere, far too close for comfort, someone was looking his way.

He knew before he even met their gaze.

And for the first time in hours, Phainon’s smile returned—sharp, reckless, and entirely too amused.

“Well,” he muttered, “guess I’m fucked.”

Phainon’s pace quickened.

The ache in his chest hadn’t dulled—it had sharpened, fine and exacting as a blade. The further he tried to drag himself from the courtyard, the heavier the air grew around him, thick with the sacred weight of consecration, of rites older than the ground beneath his feet.

And then—it found him.

A sensation like sunlight breaking through storm clouds, holy and ancient, swept over his skin, tightening his throat. It wasn’t warmth. It wasn’t even light. It was a suffocating presence, absolute and inescapable.

He stiffened before he even turned.

“Incandescent one,” came a voice, clear and unshaken, as though spoken from the lips of a statue in a long-forgotten shrine.

Phainon grit his teeth, turned with an ease he didn’t feel.

There stood a figure draped in robes of shifting opalescence, woven with threads of starlight and mist. No weapon in hand—they didn’t need one. A radiant circlet hovered above their brow, not resting, but orbiting like a captured moon. Their hair was the color of sun-bleached bone, eyes fathomless pools of liquid silver.

A familiar he knew by reputation alone.

Cyneides of Aegiros, the Pale Grace. Born of the Fifth Vein of the Skywater. Companion to Astraion, God of Dawn’s Passing. They had walked these realms since the rivers first carved paths through stone and light. There wasn’t a creature in the pantheon who hadn’t heard their name.

Phainon schooled his expression into something pleasant, though his stomach twisted.

“Cyneides,” he greeted, inclining his head with the kind of reverence expected of someone of lesser station.

And wasn’t that always the damn way of it?

Sometimes—fleetingly, never for long—he wondered what it might’ve been like. If he hadn’t been what he was. If the threads of fate hadn’t knotted him to Mydei, or if he’d been born of something clean, of water or light or stars. Not stolen breath and half-lit places.

The thought came and went, a flicker, a phantom itch beneath his ribs.

He let it pass, like he always did.

“You shine strangely,” Cyneides murmured, gaze assessing. “There is divinity upon you, yet no origin I know. An unusual star, fallen among the others.”

“I get that a lot.”

A faint smile. A humorless thing.

Cyneides stepped closer. Phainon fought not to flinch. Every instinct screamed run, but ancient, unwritten law demanded deference.

“A Duel of Aetheris is underway,” the Pale Grace continued, gesturing to the grounds behind them. “The honor of the blessed to answer the call when summoned.” Their gaze lingered on him. “Come.”

It wasn’t a request.

Refusing would be worse.

Phainon’s throat worked around a dry swallow. A thousand excuses bloomed and died on his tongue. His mind reeled, bile sharp at the back of his throat—but he managed a smile, sharp-edged and reckless.

“Wouldn’t dream of declining.”

The words tasted like ash.

Cyneides turned, the faintest glimmer of satisfaction in their expression. Phainon followed, every step a fight against the part of him that howled in protest.

He tucked the envy, the fear, the hunger deep, behind the old grin that had gotten him through worse nights.

Alright, you bastard, he thought to himself, let’s see how much of a mess you can make before they figure out what you are.

And with that, the courtyard swallowed him whole.

Phainon followed in Cyneides’ wake, the courtyard beyond wasn’t some orderly dueling ring, nor a simple gathering of combatants. It was alive—a shifting sprawl of sacred violence, divine elegance, and ancient rites tangled into one.

There were no neat queues, no idle spectators in stands. Instead, beings gathered like storms, coalescing in natural clusters of light and color and sound. Familiar sigils shimmered overhead, ever-shifting, ancient crests and seals Phainon dimly recalled from half-read texts and drunken lectures. The emblem of Aethelogon, whose blade was said to have split the first mountain. The spiral of Nyxaris, keeper of the obsidian moons. He caught sight of the twin suns of Caeronis, the legend who single-handedly quelled the Sea of Souls.

The air reeked of old power.

Phainon passed duels already underway—though none resembled the crude brawls of mortal men. Fighters moved like silk and shadow, their blades singing, bodies wreathed in light, ichor casting sparks as it hit consecrated stone. Some duels played out in complete silence, others accompanied by choirs of unseen voices. One pair fought knee-deep in suspended water that

clung to them like mercury, while another traded strikes mid-air, wingbeats sounding like thunderclaps.

He paused as he passed a familiar name—Tharos of Lethe—locked in a circling bout with Veyne the Hollow, a wraith-like figure rumored to have been born from the grief of a dying god. Their swords moved in intricate, almost reverent patterns, neither seeming eager to land the first strike, as if the duel itself was the true offering.

And despite himself, despite the gnawing ache and the too-tight relic searing against his skin, Phainon allowed a tired smile.

“Well… if I’m already doomed,” he murmured under his breath, “might as well enjoy the show.”

He trailed his gaze up to the skyless dome overhead, where shimmering vaults of bioluminescent clouds swirled like painted gods watching from above, and allowed himself a brief, unguarded moment of awe.

Thalorionis.

What a cursedly beautiful place to die.

By the time an indeterminate number of duels had passed—though really, what even was time in a place like this—Phainon was internally screaming.

He’d been stuck orbiting the bloodless, holy chaos for what felt like years. The so-called friendly sparring never seemed to stop. No one here ran out of breath. No one tired. Limbs moved like storm winds, strikes landed with the force of falling constellations, and still, no one even looked winded.

What the fuck are they on? Phainon thought, barely suppressing the urge to start gnawing at his own knuckles. The aching hunger in his chest had dulled to something raw and ancient, the kind of bone-deep craving even Incubi weren’t meant to endure for long—and still, he forced a languid, indifferent smirk onto his face.

He’d been doing his best to stay behind the bigger names, avoiding any match-ups, finding excuses about observing styles and “assessing potential threats” whenever someone got too curious. It worked. Barely.

But even Phainon knew this wasn’t sustainable. Sooner or later, someone important was going to call him out, and relic or not, if they figured out what he actually was, he’d be thrown to the Astrothes at the gate, stripped of whatever name remained of him, and left to rot in some half-flooded ruin.

And then, like a gift from whichever petty, spiteful god might be listening, it came to him.

He remembered an old tradition. One of those dusty, ancient customs half these relic-blooded zealots still held sacred. “The Rite of Aristeion’s Mercy.” Sounded pretty, sounded noble—but essentially, it meant if a duelist bested a chosen opponent named for the hour, they could invoke the rite to step down and be granted an early departure, free of offense.

The trick was, the hour’s chosen changed constantly, based on the position of the Aether lamps overhead. One look told him it had shifted to Veyne the Hollow, not someone most would volunteer to spar with.

But for Phainon, it was either that or bleed black in front of a divine audience.

“Well then,” he sighed, stretching his arms over his head and cracking his neck. His bones felt too light, his skin too tight—like his own hunger was scraping at his insides with hooked nails. Still, his grin sharpened.

He licked his lips, tasting salt and something metallic.

“Time to work.”

With as much swagger as his exhausted, half-cursed form could muster, Phainon stepped forward, offering a casual bow as if this was all a joke he was about to play at someone else’s expense.

“Veyne, darling,” he called, voice like silk over a dagger’s edge. “I believe it’s your hour.”

There was a faint hush—not a sudden stillness, no dramatic halt of the duels around them, but a collective pause in tempo. The kind of intangible shift only gods and those born too close to the divine could sense. Like the turning of a vast, invisible eye.

Veyne, draped in layered silk that shimmered like frostbitten mist, tilted their head toward him. Pale, near-translucent features unreadable, the air around them glimmered faintly, warping like heat haze.

They repeated the word softly, like tasting it.

“Darling…?”

Not anger. Just curiosity, as if Phainon had spoken a word from a long-dead tongue.

Phainon smiled wider, not because he meant it, but because instinct made him dangerous when cornered. He rolled his wrist, adopting a languid duelist’s stance—crooked but balanced, weight on the balls of his feet. The aching in his bones went ignored.

“Your hour,” he said. “Let’s make it interesting.”

Veyne didn’t move. They didn’t have to. The space around them folded. The pearlescent light warped, and then they were no longer standing across the courtyard but in front of him—a flicker, a shiver of something ancient pressing against Phainon’s skin like a storm tide.

Good gods, he thought. No wonder no one volunteers.

Then everything happened at once.

Veyne moved, an arc of their wrist, and the ground beneath Phainon splintered—not stone but light itself, shattering in jagged shards. Phainon ducked low, a flare of searing white slicing the air where his throat had

been, kicking off from the cracked pearl-dust flooring and launching himself sideways.

He hit the ground, rolled, and came up with a burst of momentum, fingertips skimming the ground to launch himself forward. His body screamed against the motion—hunger, exhaustion, fraying relic charms all threatening to give—but muscle memory had always been his most loyal sin.

His shoulder collided with Veyne mid-strike. A ripple of energy burst out, both of them thrown apart by the sheer backlash.

Phainon landed hard, spat out a curse, and drew a line in the air with two fingers. Sparks followed. A trick Mydei hated when he used—too reckless, too crude—but it worked.

The spark ignited the thin layer of sanctified mist between them into a burst of hissing light. It wouldn’t wound Veyne, but it obscured him long enough for Phainon to dart close, strike low at their leg, then pivot away, avoiding the retaliating sweep of a shimmering sleeve that cut through the space like a blade.

The crowd stirred, voices rising, not cheering—this wasn’t that kind of duel —but murmuring in approval.

Phainon grinned, blood tasting like iron at the back of his throat.

Veyne appeared again, sudden as thought, a whisper of cloth and cold radiance. A palm thrust toward his chest—a strike that would unmake lesser things.

Phainon twisted, felt the hit graze his ribs, pressure cracking something inside. His vision flashed black at the edges. Didn’t matter.

He caught Veyne’s wrist as they passed, using the momentum to spin them both, slamming a knee up into their midsection. Not much force behind it— like kicking smoke—but enough to stagger.

He pounced, hands finding purchase on the ethereal, half-real form and driving them down in a sweep, sending both tumbling.

They landed, breathless. Phainon’s hand was at Veyne’s throat—not a killing grip, but enough to count.

“I yield the hour,” Veyne murmured, serene as water.

Phainon didn’t release immediately, panting, his own heartbeat thunderous in his skull. Then, reluctantly, he let go, pushing himself upright on unsteady legs. The ache in his gut was worse now, black spots dancing behind his eyes.

The duels hadn’t stopped. The gods didn’t pause for long. But a few glances marked him now—a few knowing looks.

Veyne, impossibly, smiled.

“Well fought, angel-born.”

Phainon forced a smile. “I get to leave now, right?”

Veyne gave a shallow nod, vanishing in a ripple of cold light.

And Phainon straightened, pain and victory mingling bitterly in his chest. Now, all he had to do was make it to the gates without collapsing.

Phainon moved through the thinning courtyard flexing his fingers once, twice, adjusting the relic’s weight against his chest—the charm flickering faintly, threads of foreign light pulsing with each breath he took.

A satisfied grin tugged at his lips.

For the first time in what felt like forever, they had stared at him.

Not in revulsion. Not in veiled contempt. Not as a shadow trailing behind some greater thing. No—recognition. Measured. Appraising.

It hit him a few paces after he started walking. Subtle, but sharp.

They saw me.

And damn it, it felt good.

Not enough to fix anything, but enough to make his steps a little lighter, shoulders a little straighter as he ambled toward the nearest archway leading to the outer causeways. He was already working out half a dozen escape routes in his head, each more impossible than the last, but optimism was a dangerous and addictive thing when you hadn’t tasted it in years.

“Alright,” he muttered under his breath, hands in his pockets, dodging a cluster of Aetherborn glassfish darting overhead, “maybe a clean break through the lower sanctum. Nobody bothers checking relic signatures down there. Worst case, swim it. Hope the Astrothes are still on their millennia nap.”

A self-amused chuckle slipped past his lips. His humor was usually all teeth, sharp and defensive, but now it was loose. Actual amusement.

He tipped his head back, stretching, feeling his spine pop satisfyingly, when the air shifted.

Not dramatically. Not the crashing silence of divine wrath.

Just colder.

A thin, invisible thread of frost trailing down his spine. The kind of feeling you got when walking into a room you swore was empty—but someone’s already inside.

His stride didn’t break. If anything, it got a little more careless.

Never show it.

That was lesson one.

The cold settled. Stayed. Every instinct in him begged to glance over his shoulder, but instead, he yawned, rubbing at the side of his face, palm dragging down the curve of his cheek lazily.

And then he felt it.

Wet.

Warm.

Brows furrowing, Phainon let his hand drop to eye level. Blinked.

A smear of black across his fingers. Viscous. Iridescent in the soft light, tinged faintly violet where it caught the shimmer of the sanctified mist overhead.

Blood.

And not just any blood.

His blood.

Black.

Time cracked open.

For one terrible, beautiful moment, the world shrank to the space between his heartbeat and the next. He couldn’t remember getting hit. Couldn’t remember bleeding. But it didn’t matter.

Because this wasn’t supposed to happen.

Not here.

Not now.

His heart gave a painful, stuttering lurch against his ribs.

Shit.

The blood still shimmered on his fingertips.

A memory of all those watching eyes slid back into his mind, and this time it wasn’t recognition of a peer. It was recognition of a mistake. A wrong thing.

Phainon swallowed, throat dry.

The cold deepened.

And now, now, it was time to run.

The air—if you could even call it that, this consecrated weight of divine mists and ancient salt—pressed heavy against his skin.

Okay. Okay. No one saw. No one saw.

His fingers curled into a fist, smearing the dark stain across his palm.

It was fine. He’d been sweating, right? Old bruises, old cuts—this place was a hazard for mortals anyway. Maybe it wasn’t even his. Maybe—

A bead of sweat slid down the side of his temple.

He didn’t wipe it.

Instead, with the casual care of someone who absolutely wasn’t two seconds from internally losing his shit, Phainon turned, took a slow step toward the nearest side passage. A smooth, gleaming corridor of polished coral and pale-light glyphs, leading deeper into the tiered sanctums.

He kept his head down. Not slouched—never slouched—but unremarkable. Forgettable. One face in a city of myths.

Another step.

The air was a knife against his skin now, the thin hum of old enchantments brushing against the relic at his throat like searching fingers.

The sigils along the arches he passed flickered.

Only for a moment.

He almost missed it.

His stomach dropped.

No one saw.

He repeated it like a prayer, though it tasted sour in his mouth.

And then—

A soft, wet drip echoed onto the pearlescent floor.

He didn’t look.

Didn’t need to.

Another drop followed.

And another.

Phainon’s pulse thundered in his ears.

A few feet ahead, a slender figure veiled in streaming silver silk paused, as if catching a scent on the air. They turned their head, pale irises glinting like twin moons. A hush fell over the mist.

Not silence.

A hush.

The kind you felt more than heard.

Like the deep pressure before a storm breaks open.

Phainon swore under his breath. A sharp, ugly sound.

Time to go.

He pivoted on his heel—and something cold brushed the back of his neck. Not a hand. Not a blade. Something worse. He doesn’t dare look back.

The remnants of old fear from darker days, sewn deep into his marrow, came screaming to the surface. His breath hitched. Every instinct he’d buried for years, polished into civility and smirking nonchalance, cracked open.

He ran.

Not a sprint.

A calculated, clean break.

Fluid, almost casual, as though he was simply moving faster because he had somewhere to be.

He slipped down a narrow corridor flanked by towering statues of drowned titans, each one cloaked in salt-crusted chains.

The mist churned behind him.

He didn’t look back.

Wouldn’t.

His teeth clenched. His pulse was a frantic snare beat in his skull.

“Shit, shit, shit—” he hissed between clenched teeth, sliding one hand into his coat for the dagger hilt at his hip, more a charm than a weapon in a place like this.

Another pulse of cold.

This time, it came with a voice.

Soft. Silk-draped. Amused.

“Leaving so soon?”

And just like that—

The world cracked open.

Golden threads.

Not strands. Not silk.

Not rope.

Threads.

Fine as mist, gleaming like the first light of dawn, searing where they touched skin—they snapped into place around Phainon’s frame before he could take another step.

A low, wordless hum filled the corridor. The air grew impossibly heavier, the very marrow of the sanctum responding. Even the mist stilled, as though it, too, knew better.

And then she was there.

Aglaea.

Descending like a sunbeam fractured through ancient waters, her presence more felt than seen at first—a warmth that wasn’t warmth, a weight of divinity so clean and composed it made other gods seem like petulant children clamoring for attention.

Her voice followed. Smooth. Calm. But edged like a dagger drawn in quiet halls.

“You disappoint me, Phainon.”

A simple statement.

No dramatics.

No raised voice.

But it landed like a blow.

Phainon froze, tension locked tight across his shoulders. A muscle twitched in his jaw as he lifted his chin—the mask slipping back into place with practiced ease.

He grinned.

Not too wide.

“Disappointment? I was aiming for mild inconvenience, actually. Should’ve known I’d overshoot.”

His tone was light, breezy—but it rang hollow even to him. The cold sweat beneath his collar betrayed him, as did the tightness behind his eyes.

Aglaea stepped closer, the threads tightening just enough to remind him they could crush him into ash at a thought.

But they didn’t.

Her lips quirked. Barely.

The faintest ghost of a smile, though it held no warmth.

“I should leave you to the Astrothes,” she mused, as though considering a troublesome child’s punishment. “Or better yet… Tartarus’ archons would love to hear your explanation.”

A bead of sweat slid down Phainon’s neck.

He swallowed.

“Not that I wouldn’t cherish a scenic trip to the Pit, but… given the circumstances, I was hoping for something a little less eternal torment-y. You know. A firm lecture. Maybe a ceremonial flogging. I’m flexible.”

He forced another grin, but his gaze didn’t quite meet hers.

Because behind the humor—behind every flicker of deflection and wit—sat that cold, ugly thing.

The weight of what he was.

Not a god. Not a hero.

An incubi. A familiar. The kind of creature most gods spat at in passing.

But tethered to the only name he’d ever wanted to follow.

And now they all knew.

That ancient, sour sting curled low in his gut. He hated how easy it was to feel it. To remember what it meant, here, of all places.

Aglaea’s gaze softened by a fraction—not pity. Never pity.

Something else.

She raised a hand, fingers brushing the air. The threads loosened.

“You’ll get no Tartarus, Phainon,” she said quietly. “I have something far more fitting in mind.”

She turned, the threads drawing him effortlessly after, like a puppet on golden string.

And though his chest ached and his pride stung raw, he found—despite everything—he was almost relieved it had been her.

Anyone else, and he wouldn’t be breathing.

And that’s how he ended up here.

Phainon sat slumped in his seat, shoulders hunched like a kid hauled before the village elder for stealing the ceremonial wine—except swap ‘elder’ for

a room full of living myths who could obliterate stars with a passing thought.

This was the Agnostherion.

The Place of Unmasking.

A sanctum few ever saw, and none left unchanged. The vaulted dome above shimmered like an overturned night sky, constellations lazily drifting through misty air. Lightless braziers burned silver flame, and the thrones weren’t just seats—they were monuments, each etched with names the world no longer dared speak aloud.

And sitting upon them were the ones responsible for making history happen.

Phainon could feel them watching him.

Not cruelly, not even with disdain.

Just the weight of beings so ancient, so vast, that existing near them felt like standing at the edge of a cliff, staring into eternity.

And there, at the highest seat—not in judgment, but in cold disbelief—sat Mydei.

Not scowling. Not furious.

Just staring.

The Crown Prince of Heaven’s gaze was a thing Phainon had grown accustomed to over the years. Usually sharp with dry amusement or heavy with fond, exhausted patience.

Right now?

It was an expression caught somewhere between what the actual fuck are you doing here and how did you survive long enough to get caught?

Phainon felt himself sink lower in his chair, heat prickling under his skin. It wasn’t fear—not with Mydei. Never with him.

It was mortification.

Because if it were anyone else, he could’ve laughed it off, spun a ridiculous excuse, charmed his way out.

But Mydei?

He actually… cared what that bastard thought of him.

Phainon hadn’t looked up since the moment he got hauled into this place, and he sure as hell wasn’t about to start now.

Aglaea, seated beside him, looked completely unbothered. Sipping her tea like she was perched in her favorite garden arbor and not the most feared judgment hall in existence.

Finally, she set the cup down with a pleasant, delicate clink. The sound echoed across marble and stone.

A beat.

Then she spoke, voice silk-wrapped steel.

“Now,” Aglaea said with a faint, not-unkind smile that made Phainon’s stomach sink, “let’s begin, shall we?”
