It hadn’t started like this.

The Agnostherion—a chamber built into the marrow of the world, where ancient names were unmade and woven into legend—had convened for something important. Something grand. Phainon vaguely remembered Aglaea murmuring about “matters of celestial order” while dragging him here by the proverbial ear.

Now?

It was a tribunal.

His.

“How dare a being of your nature desecrate Thalarionis?” one of them spat, voice like shattering ice against marble. A severe figure, all opalescent skin

and hair braided in threads of starlight, glaring down at him from an ivory seat.

Another leaned in, lips curling. “This is precisely why Incubi should never have been permitted to exist.”

Oh. Well. Damn.

Phainon stood very still, shoulders slumped in something between fatigue and resignation. He kept his eyes forward, careful not to glance at the seat where Mydei sat, radiating a brand of silent fury that was somehow worse than if he’d spoken.

Someone else—a withered thing that looked like it had personally salted the earth after the fall of the Titans—sneered, “Parasite.”

Tainted familiar.

Lesser breed.

The words hit like pebbles against glass. Small, sharp things. The kind you’d barely register until your skin stung from the accumulation. Phainon wasn’t new to this. Gods had never been subtle in their contempt. He just hadn’t expected it to be so… colorful this early in the day.

Well, this is worse than expected.

His gaze flicked to the grand arched doorway behind him, briefly calculating the distance, the guards, the ceiling height. If I bolt now… I can probably swim to the surface before they catch me. Fake my death. Change my name. Open a roadside eel stall somewhere deepsea. It wouldn’t be the worst plan I’ve had.

Another voice chimed in, syrupy-sweet, as if they were doing him a kindness. “Of course, one cannot entirely blame the creature. It is in their nature. That hunger. That filth.”

Phainon sighed internally. Gods, you people are exhausting.

And this was only the beginning.

A voice older than sand rasped from somewhere near the back. “I never trusted Philemon, not since the incident at the Obsidian Shore.”

A pause.

Phainon blinked. “Who?”

Another decrepit figure, this one looking like the fossilized remains of a half-forgotten war deity, jabbed a gnarled finger in his direction. “You. You’re the one who seduced the entire Monastery of Selene during the Fourth Aeon, aren’t you? Blighted every altar. Disgraced a hundred vows.”

Phainon opened his mouth, then slowly closed it. What in the hell was that even supposed to mean?

“Wasn’t me,” he muttered, loud enough for Aglaea to hear. She didn’t so much as blink, delicately sipping her tea.

Another god, hair like coiled mist and eyes that shimmered like a dying star, squinted down at him. “Feanor?”

“I—” Phainon dragged a hand down his face. “Phainon.”

At this point, he threw a subtle glance toward the high seat.

Mydei’s expression hadn’t changed. Still sharp, still unreadable. But there was the faintest twitch at the corner of his mouth, somewhere between ‘I’ll kill them all’ and ‘this is why I hate these meetings.’

Phainon side-eyed him harder. Are you hearing this?

He swore, for half a heartbeat, Mydei’s gaze flicked to him—a silent, ‘Of course I’m hearing this.’

And then right back to stony, simmering silence.

Another ancient god leaned forward. “Are you not one of Echidna’s spawn?”

“What the f—no!”

A strangled noise from the seat beside him. Aglaea coughed delicately into her cup, but Phainon caught the flicker of amusement in her eyes.

Gods. This was going to be a long meeting.

The shift was subtle at first. The usual pompous sneering and mispronunciations bleeding into something crueler.

“I see no reason this…creature…should retain the mark of a familiar,” one god announced, voice like cracked marble. “It was a mistake to elevate an Incubi to such standing in the first place.”

A ripple of murmured assent followed. Another, draped in sea-silver cloth, flicked an elegant hand. “Exile would be mercy.”

Phainon stiffened. Well okay. Guess we’re escalating now.

“I move for cleansing,” someone else drawled, and the word made his stomach twist. He knew what cleansing meant, and it wasn’t metaphorical.

Okay, he needed to speak now.

Phainon cleared his throat and rose halfway from his seat, managing a polite smile so thin it practically cracked. “With all due respect, venerable ones,” his voice steady but edging toward sharp, “I didn’t desecrate anything. I didn’t seduce any monasteries—recently—and I certainly didn’t blight your godsforsaken altars.”

A low, scandalized murmur.

“I entered on sanctioned grounds, under relic seal. Participated in the rites of Aetheris as per tradition. And, let’s be honest, outperformed half your blessed little champions while doing it.”

Another ripple, this time mixed with outrage.

Aglaea raised a brow over her teacup, clearly impressed.

“Furthermore,” Phainon pressed on, his polite facade straining at the edges, “I have upheld every term of my binding. If my mere existence offends your ancient sensibilities, perhaps you should revisit the laws you wrote yourselves.”

He was panting by the end of it, teeth gritted behind a brittle grin. A cold sweat beading at his temple.

Silence hung heavy.

He darted a glance toward Mydei again, as if silently begging any time now would be great.

But the Crown Prince of the Heavens remained where he was, sharp gaze locked on him like a hawk sizing up a particularly reckless hare. Unreadable.

And gods, it burned.

Another voice, low and venomous: “Parasite.”

A second: “Tainted breed.”

Phainon’s jaw twitched. He felt his composure start to fray like overstrained thread.

Just a little longer, he told himself. Just hold it together.

But the bile in his throat tasted like old shame and godblood.

The council chamber simmered with tension thick enough to choke on. Another insult dangled in the air, another self-righteous voice drawing breath—when a voice cut through it.

Cold. Low. Absolute.

“He bested your chosen, didn’t he?”

Silence.

The words rolled through the chamber like a chill wave, sinking sharp and deep. Every head turned toward the high dais where Mydei lounged—or rather, sat with the predatory stillness of a blade half-drawn. His hand rested against his cheek, expression the very definition of unimpressed.

One of the elder gods bristled, pride twitching to life. But Mydei’s gaze flicked toward them—a slow, disinterested pass of icy golden eyes.

They went quiet. Sat down.

Phainon, against his better judgment, felt his stomach flip. He knew that look. He knew what followed it. And by the gods, it wasn’t for anyone else’s sake.

“Strange,” Mydei went on, voice all lazy frostbite, “for a ‘lesser creature.’”

A single, sharp-edged pause.

No one spoke. No one so much as breathed.

And just like that—the accusations shrank back. The daggers dulled.

Because if the Crown Prince of the Heavens made a claim, divine law itself bent to it. And whether Mydei admitted it aloud or not, there wasn’t a god in the room who didn’t hear the mine in that.

Phainon kept his face neutral. Barely. But inside?

He was already drafting the world’s longest what the actual fuck monologue.

Phainon, in a moment of absolutely unparalleled genius, shot Mydei a thumbs-up.

A literal, dumbass, mortal-style thumbs-up.

Across a divine council chamber.

In front of the assembled gods who quite literally decided the fates of realms.

Mydei’s jaw ticked, just a fraction. His fingers drummed once against the arm of his seat like a man contemplating smiting his own houseplant for being endearingly idiotic. His expression didn’t flicker, but Phainon felt the unimpressed, bone-deep why by the Gods do I have such a stupid familiar radiating off him in waves.

But also—and this was the stupid part, really—the unspoken his under it.

Mydei wouldn’t let anyone else take him. Never had. Never would.

Phainon swallowed. His internal monologue lit up like a funeral pyre.

Holy shit I’m saved.

A beat.

Holy shit that’s gonna cost me later.

Because Mydei never forgot a debt. And he collected with interest.

Aglaea, unbothered, set her teacup down with a delicate clink, smiling as though none of this had just happened.

“Well,” she said brightly, “shall we continue?”

Phainon slumped further into his chair.

By the stars, I should’ve faked my death when I had the chance.

The atmosphere in the Agnostherion was still sour, but noticeably muted now, like a storm forced to simmer under a watchful sun. Mydei’s words had landed like an executioner’s blade, and the room knew better than to test the weight of it twice.

A few of the older gods—the ones so ancient even their memories had rusted—grudgingly cleared their throats, muttering half-hearted retractions that didn’t fool anyone.

“Perhaps… we spoke in haste.”

“A misjudgment… of lineage.”

Aglaea, ever the tactician in a silk glove, smiled like she hadn’t just witnessed the entire room consider public execution five minutes ago. She folded her hands with effortless poise, voice as smooth as consecrated oil. “Let it be recorded, then, that Phainon, familiar of the Crown Prince, displayed… unexpected prowess. And a unique resilience under divine pressure.”

Phainon, who’d been doing his best impression of an inanimate object for the past ten minutes, mentally translated that with a grim little snort.

‘Cockroach.’ She just called me a cockroach.

He fought the urge to smirk. Mostly because if he cracked a grin now, one of the old bastards would probably keel over from the sheer audacity.

Aglaea gave him a brief, knowing glance.

Mydei remained leaned back in his seat, silent and lethal as ever—but Phainon swore he saw the faintest ghost of a smirk tug at the corner of his mouth.

Just for a moment.

Then it was gone.

The verdict came down like a closing blade.

“He will not be punished here,” one of the elder councilors finally conceded, words acidic in his mouth. “His… patron will answer for him.”

A few murmurs stirred at that—but no one dared challenge it now.

Mydei, still seated in regal detachment, raised his hand with casual finality. “I’ll take responsibility.”

The council fell silent once more.

Aglaea, amused as ever, started speaking at that moment. “Good. Then this matter is resolved. Recession is called.”

The gathering broke apart like frost under sunlight—gods and ancient familiars rising and vanishing in flashes of light and vapor. Only Mydei remained for a moment longer, before turning without a word and striding out through one of the arching exits.

Phainon didn’t need to be told. The man moved like a storm cloud with a sense of purpose. He trailed after him.

The doors of the Agnostherion closed behind them with a muted thrum.

He barely had time to blink before a hand snatched his arm and yanked him into a narrow side corridor, the divine equivalent of a backstage alley. A solid wall of Mydei loomed over him, golden eyes sharp and unamused.

“What,” Mydei said, voice low and lethal, “were you doing in Thalarionis?”

There wasn’t rage in his tone. Not the kind that would crack marble. It was something else. Concern. The kind that didn’t surface often but hit twice as hard when it did.

Phainon stared up at him, feeling the telltale prickle of heat crawl up his neck. He should’ve expected this. Honestly, he kinda did. What he didn’t expect was how close Mydei had him pinned against the wall, one arm braced just beside his head, their bodies mere inches apart.

“Wow,” Phainon breathed, tilting his head with a grin. “Didn’t know you cared, Your Highness.”

Mydei didn’t blink. “I don’t.”

The lie was so barefaced it made Phainon grin wider, despite the fact that his pulse was going haywire in his throat.

“Sure you don’t,” he murmured, eyes half-lidded. “And here I thought you only got this rough when I asked nicely.”

Mydei’s expression didn’t change, but there was a flicker. Something sharp and frustrated in those gilded eyes.

“You could’ve died,” he said flatly. “You should’ve, with the Month of Aetheris upon us. Did you forget what happened last time you crossed aether-saturated ground? Or did you just stop caring whether you live through the cycle?”

Phainon faltered for half a second. He hated that. Hated how easily Mydei could carve through all the shit and find the marrow of him.

“I was careful,” he lied.

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“Am not.”

“Are.”

Phainon snorted softly, feeling some of the tension bleed out of him, though his heart was still hammering from… well, everything. He let his head loll back against the wall, a sigh escaping.

“I needed out,” he muttered. “And it was either sneak into a cursed underwater city or let my brain melt outside waiting for you all alone. I took my chances.”

Mydei exhaled, a long-suffering sound, and finally stepped back—not far, but enough for Phainon to breathe properly.

“I should chain you to your quarters.”

“Ooh,” Phainon perked up, trailing after him as Mydei turned and started walking again. “Promises, promises.”

Mydei cast him a deadpan look over one shoulder.

Phainon coughed. “So… about those punishments you mentioned back there—”

“You’ll live,” Mydei said, no inflection, but there was a flash of something in his gaze before he looked away again. A tightness in his jaw. A weight in his posture.

And for a moment, Phainon sobered. Because beneath all the snark and royal irritation, Mydei had been worried. Not for his familiar’s reputation. Not for protocol.

For him.

Phainon let the teasing drop just enough to let that warmth sit in his chest for a moment. Then, because he was who he was:

“Can I at least pick the restraints?”

Mydei kept walking, but the faint twitch at the corner of his mouth was answer enough.

Phainon followed, smiling like an idiot.

The council chamber’s vast doors opened once more, spilling pale celestial light across the marble floor as gods, spirits, and familiars filtered out in murmuring clusters. The air still felt thick with leftover judgment, but no one dared meet Phainon’s gaze now. A few familiars dipped respectful nods to Mydei as he passed, others wisely keeping their heads bowed, the tension of earlier transmuted into wary, grudging deference.

Phainon trailed a few steps behind, still mentally recovering from the fact that he wasn’t exiled, beheaded, or turned into divine lawn fertilizer.

It wasn’t until they crossed the final threshold of the Agnostherion that Mydei slowed, an unreadable look flickering across his face. He stopped just before the threshold of the outer courtyard, golden eyes fixed ahead but something else tightening in his jaw.

Phainon cocked a brow. “What? Don’t tell me you forgot your diadem or something.”

Mydei didn’t answer at first. Then, with a faint exhale, he spoke—voice soft, so only Phainon could hear.

“…Let’s stay a bit longer.”

Phainon blinked. “Wait—what?”

“You wanted to see this place properly, didn’t you?” Mydei kept his gaze forward, tone carefully neutral, but his hand reached out—not the grip from before, no threading of golden light, no pressure. Just a hand, extended, open. Waiting.

Phainon’s heart did a weird little flip. Not because of the offer. Not because the Crown Prince of the Heavens was casually suggesting they loiter in a sanctified divine city like it was no big deal. But because for once, for once, it wasn’t duty or power making the decision.

It was for him.

He hesitated half a beat. Then, without his usual teasing quip, he reached out and took Mydei’s hand.

Warm. Steady. Certain.

And like that, the ache in his chest dulled a little. His steps felt lighter.

“Lead the way, Your Highness,” Phainon murmured, voice sardonic but softer than usual.

And together, hand in hand, they walked back into the divine city.

The sanctum of Mydei was less a residence and more a celestial bastion—a place where the heavens folded close and ancient, star-carved halls hummed with a power too old for names. Constellations crawled lazily across the vaulted expanse overhead, shifting with the seasons, their light pooling in pale, opalescent rivers along polished starstone floors.

It wasn’t a place most beings visited lightly. And yet, Phainon had his own room, gifted by the Crown prince himself.

Currently, he wasn’t in it.

He was somewhere higher—a place where wide, open terraces unfurled like the palm of a sleeping titan, high above the sanctum’s inner sanctuaries. It wasn’t a roof, because nothing in Celestialis was so mundane. No—this was

a stargazer’s platform, once used by the early court to chart the celestial shifts before mortal astronomy stole half their secrets. The marble here was warm to the touch, veined with lines of liquid silver that pulsed with the seasons.

Phainon lay sprawled across it like a discarded poem, one leg hooked over the side, half-lidded gaze tracking a constellation he didn’t care enough to name.

He was bored.

The kind of thick, damned boredom only immortals could truly appreciate —stretched thin by an eternal afternoon, worn raw by too many days of good behavior. And worse yet, it was still the Month of Aetheris.

He flicked a pebble—or what passed for a pebble here, a tiny shard of crystallized starlight—at a nearby krater resting too elegantly on a ledge it had no business being on. Ancient, hand-thrown, ringed in depictions of battles long since reduced to myths even among their kind.

It struck true.

The vessel tipped with a delicate wobble, then fell. Phainon didn’t even flinch at the shattering sound—a low, musical crack that split the charged air. A beat later, and the scattered fragments slowed, halting mid-air in a shimmer of white-gold light before lazily reassembling themselves. The krater floated back to its ledge as if nothing had happened.

Phainon beamed to himself.

“Still got it.”

He gave a low, satisfied hum and flopped onto his back again, hands laced behind his head. Somewhere deep below, he could sense Mydei moving —a pulse, a flicker of cold radiance in the sanctum’s heart. Probably reviewing decrees or attending to some other infuriatingly responsible task while Phainon wasted away from celestial abstinence.

The thought made his grin widen, though it felt more like a grimace now.

Aetheris. Gods help him.

And it was only getting worse.

He threw an arm over his face to block out the drifting stars, knowing full well he wouldn’t last the night.

Not like this.

Phainon leans back against the sun-warmed stone, the ache beneath his skin constant now. He could feel the month’s pressure gnawing at him, a dull, needling pain he tried to ignore.

What to do, what to do…

The gardens?

He didn’t care much for sentimental flora unless they tried to eat him.

The Archives?

“Absolutely not.”

If he wanted judgmental stares from long-dead names, he’d have stayed in the Agnostherion.

The baths, maybe—

Tempting. But last time he nearly got burned by the water, and the water sprits there…no further comment.

And then it struck him.

The Sunset Vigils.

Quiet. Untouched. Serene. The one place in Celestialis no one badgered him.

Phainon straightened, rolling his neck with a muted crack.

“Perfect.”

He slipped off the ledge, boots ghosting over the marble, the sanctum’s divine light catching in his hair like liquid sun. Hunger still gnawed at him —but for now, it could wait. It always had to wait.

The Sunset Vigils would do.

The halls of Celestialis stretched around him, vast as a world entire. Ceilings soared higher than any mortal mountain, vaulted with sunfire and living starstone. Every step he took echoed against marble older than recorded history, the air thick with the scent of ozone and sun-warmed mineral.

He passed a mural floating midair, its paint rippling like water —a battle long since ended, gods clashing with a horde of nameless things made of shadow and teeth. One of the figures in the mural looked suspiciously like Mydei, young and furious, hurling a star like a spear.

A harp played itself in an alcove, fingers of invisible light plucking notes so mournful even the stone seemed to hum in sympathy. It had been playing that same tune for two centuries. Phainon didn’t know why. Didn’t care either. He gave it a lazy two-fingered salute as he strolled by.

A mosaic of the First Dawn spread across a domed ceiling ahead, a wash of molten gold and bleeding pink, celestial figures rising from the void. Phainon craned his neck to look up at it as he passed —partly admiring the craft, mostly because his back ached like hell and he needed an excuse to stretch.

Divine figures moved through the halls around him. A goddess with stormcloud hair and skin the color of distant lightning inclined her head to him in passing. He offered a smile, half flirt, half challenge. She didn’t bother stopping.

A demigod leaned against a pillar, polishing a celestial spear until it gleamed like a captured sun. The bastard barely gave Phainon a glance, though the corner of his mouth twitched —whether in disdain or irritation, Phainon couldn’t tell. He waved anyway.

Then there was that familiar. The one he’d beaten a few weeks back in the duel to avoid suspicion, left flat on the floor and humiliated before a ring of snickering peers. Phainon caught his eye, smirked, and the poor fool immediately looked away, pretending to be absolutely fascinated by the decorative etching of a serpent devouring the sky.

Serves you right, Phainon thought smugly, rolling his shoulders. Here, away from the suffocating holiness of Thalarionis and the Council’s venomous stares, he could afford to be a little more himself —sharp-edged, irreverent, and so profoundly done with the gods and their melodrama.

Somewhere ahead, he could already hear the muted chants of the Sunset Vigils. Good. He needed it.

And maybe, if the Fates were merciful, there’d be something worth stealing along the way.

Phainon took a turn where he shouldn’t have.

Which, in fairness, wasn’t entirely his fault. The paths of here weren’t like mortal places, where left was left and down was down. Here, the corridors moved with the seasons, stairs inverted themselves on solstices, and doors led to different realms if you opened them with the wrong hand. It was a place built for gods, and the architecture had no patience for mortals—or half-blood incubi with too much attitude and not enough sense.

He ducked through an archway framed by sun-gold laurels and immediately felt it—the unmistakable pressure of important shit happening. The air hung heavier here, thick with old rites and the weight of converging realms. Voices murmured in a dozen languages at once, and distant bells tolled in time with nothing at all.

A sprawling gallery opened before him, overlooking a confluence of star paths. Figures had gathered in clusters: towering beings cloaked in shifting constellations, envoys made of mist and starlight, high familiars wearing the banners of their patrons. At the center of it all, an obsidian dais rose like a black sun, a ceremonial nexus already alight with glyphs older than death.

Ah. Shit.

The Syzygy Convergence.

Phainon groaned internally, rubbing a hand down his face. Of course it would be this week, that explains all the guests here. The last time this happened—what, three centuries ago?—an entire minor pantheon defected, two archons declared war mid-ceremony, and a pair of sun-gods ran off together. Scandalous stuff. Good times.

But this? This was not his scene. Not unless someone was pouring wine or starting a fight.

He turned on his heel, ready to bolt—but not before a scent caught him. Sweet, heady, sharp as lightning-struck pine. A glimmer of something glinting unattended on a nearby pedestal: a delicate, sun-blessed fruit known to be wildly illegal outside consecrated rites.

Phainon’s mouth watered.

Maybe if I just—

He reached for it.

A pulse of pressure slammed into him like a hammer to the ribs. Not violent —just a casual reminder that he was very much not supposed to be here. The kind of ambient holy energy that made his incubi blood crawl and his stomach lurch.

Phainon coughed sharply, stumbling back a step. His skin prickled, breath catching as his bones ached under the weight of it.

“Right, okay, no,” he muttered to himself, throwing his hands up in surrender. “Not worth it. Not dying for a damn plum.”

He slowly pivoted backwards, heading back toward the safe familiarity of the Vigils. The path dimmed behind him as the Convergence’s radiance receded. He could still feel the sting of it in his chest, like someone had dropped a sun down his throat.

And the dumbest part? This was Mydei’s realm. He didn’t have to steal anything here. He had a whole room, a set of keys—well, okay, not keys, more like a sigil-ward—and technically full access. He could’ve asked.

He wouldn’t have, obviously. But he could have.

Phainon snorted at himself, rubbing his shoulder as he walked. This place was a labyrinth of starstone, moving skies, and the casual kind of sanctity that made his skin itch. And he liked it here. A little too much.

He liked it because it was his. Not officially, not by title or decree—but by virtue of the fact Mydei hadn’t thrown him out yet. And probably wouldn’t.

Not until he did something really stupid.

Which, given his track record, could be any minute now.

Whatever, he’ll worry about that later.

Phainon finally reached the Sunset Vigils.

A vast, open expanse carved from ancient starstone, it jutted out into the aether like a balcony to nowhere. Below it stretched the cosmic sea, a vast undulating canvas of light and shadow where constellations rippled like liquid gold, stars blinking in and out of existence like the heartbeat of the heavens. The horizon bled from violet to indigo, soft hues swallowing the sharp lines of the world.

Dais-like seats carved from meteoric stone lined the terrace, their surfaces faintly aglow with a cold, silver sheen. Incense drifted in curling threads from hanging braziers—dusk and myrrh.

And, best of all:

No one else was around.

Phainon let out a long, indulgent sigh, his shoulders finally dropping. Gods, it was perfect. No blustering emissaries, no sanctimonious priests, no overgrown walking suns. Just the dusk, the wind, and the endless sea of stars.

He flopped down onto the dias—uncaring of the faint snap of static energy against his skin—and leaned back with a groan. The stone was cool, almost soothing against the constant ache in his bones.

A rare moment of peace.

For about thirty seconds.

Then it started.

That slow, relentless burn in his chest. His skin prickled, sensitive to every mote of light. The glow in the air felt like glass scraping along his nerves.

Phainon clenched his jaw, squeezing his eyes shut.

Maybe if I just ride it out. One more day. Just a little longer.

He’d managed this long, hadn’t he? Sure, his hands shook when he reached for anything in this place, and sure, he felt like he might black out when too much hit him at once—but it wasn’t like anyone noticed. Mydei hadn’t said anything. And Phainon sure as hell wasn’t going to be the one to admit it.

He blew out a slow breath and grumbled to no one, “Dramatic bastards, the lot of ’em.”

A constellation overhead blinked, like it agreed.

Damn Month of Aetheris. Damn divine politics. Damn his own stubborn ass for thinking he could tough it out just to…what, prove himself? Outlast it? Be worthy of a god who never asked him to bleed for it?

He groaned and let his head tip back against the starlight, watching the sky ripple overhead.

“Dumbass gods and their self-importance… should’ve been a baker.”

The cosmic sea shimmered in reply.

Phainon let his gaze drift lazily along the curve of the horizon, catching glimpses of floating sanctuaries drifting through the upper reaches—pale, spired structures tethered by chains of silver light, carrying envoys between realms during the Syzygy Convergence. Every so often, one would vanish behind the veil of clouds.

In the distance, a seraphic choir was rehearsing for one of the day’s rites, their voices like glass bells struck by summer wind. It prickled at the edges of his hearing, both beautiful and headache-inducing.

He made a face.

He felt it before he saw him.

A subtle shift in the air, like the crackle of a coming storm. That same pressure that made the skin on the back of his neck prickle, the taste of charged energy thick on his tongue. It was like sensing a wildfire cresting the next hill—not dangerous to him, not really, but impossible to ignore.

And then there he was.

Mydei.

Leaning against one of the starstone pillars, expression caught somewhere between unimpressed and resigned. Dressed in red, sleeveless silks trimmed in muted gold, hair tousled like it always was when he couldn’t be bothered, gaze sharp as a falling blade. The ambient glow of the sanctum bent subtly

around him—the weight of him making the space ripple like heat above a flame.

He exhaled, long-suffering, and crossed the distance in a few measured steps before dropping down onto the bench beside Phainon.

“So this is where you’ve been sulking.”

Phainon grunted without looking at him, gaze fixed on the cosmic sea. “Sulking’s dramatic. I prefer ‘heroically enduring.’”

“Enduring what, precisely? The unbearable burden of not being the loudest one in the room for once?”

“Mm. The oppressive injustice of radiant gods judging me for my unparalleled charm.”

A flicker of something almost resembling a smirk tugged at Mydei’s mouth, though his eyes stayed sharp—assessing. It wasn’t just banter. Phainon could feel the weight of his gaze, the way it lingered too long on the tightness in his jaw, the fine sheen of sweat on his skin despite the cool night air, the way his hand flexed as though to steady himself.

“Phainon.”

He hated how Mydei said his name sometimes.

Phainon cracked a grin that felt too sharp. “What, miss me already?”

Mydei didn’t answer right away. The dusk light caught on the lines of his face, making him look older than his agelessness ever allowed—not weary, exactly, but weathered in a way no one else could see. He tilted his head, watching Phainon in a way that made it hard to breathe.

“You’re overdrawn.”

“Tch. I’ve been worse.”

“That’s not something to brag about.”

“It is if you’ve lived through it.”

Silence stretched between them.

Phainon finally sighed, tipping his head back. “It’s nothing. I can handle it.”

“You shouldn’t have to.”

Another beat of silence.

Phainon snorted, bitter. “You don’t get it.”

Mydei’s gaze didn’t waver. “Then explain it to me.”

But Phainon didn’t. Not yet.

Because it was easier to deflect. To grin like the insufferable bastard he was born to be, and pretend the hollow gnawing inside him wasn’t clawing its way up his throat.

He settled for, “You’re a persistent little storm cloud, you know that?”

“You’re in my sanctum. Don’t tempt me to throw you off the balcony.”

“That’s flirting where I’m from.”

That earned a faint, exasperated sound from Mydei, but not a denial.

And for a moment—just a moment—the ache in Phainon’s chest dulled once again.

Mydei didn’t speak right away, and Phainon felt the shift again—that subtle ripple in the air.

“You didn’t show for the Syzygy.”

Phainon snorted, leaning his head back against the cool stone behind him. “Not exactly my scene. All those sanctimonious pricks posturing for power,

waxing poetic about eternal balance while half of them are plotting how to screw the other half sideways? I’ll pass.”

A pause. He felt Mydei’s gaze still on him. Too piercing, concerned.

Phainon sighed. Ran a hand through his hair, fingers snagging in the light strands.

“Alright, fine.” The words tasted worse than he expected. “Didn’t wanna… embarrass you.”

Mydei’s brow lifted a fraction, unreadable. “Embarrass me?”

“Yeah, you know.” Phainon clicked his tongue, thinking of how to put it. “Not exactly what most picture when they think ‘favored familiar of the Crown Prince.’ Thought maybe if I stayed scarce, let you shine without the parasite clinging to your heels, it’d make your life easier.”

The silence that followed wasn’t empty. It was dense. Heavy with things unsaid, things better left unsaid, and things long overdue.

Mydei moved then—not much, just straightened a little, but the shift in his presence was like watching the sky darken.

His voice, when it came, was steady. Measured like the strike of a sword.

“You are my familiar.”

Phainon blinked.

“Mine,” Mydei repeated, quieter now. “And if anyone in any realm dares imply you aren’t worthy of that bond—I’ll carve their tongues from their skulls and feed them to something hungry.”

A beat.

“Or better yet,” he added, almost lazily, though the ardent tone in his voice said otherwise, “you can do it yourself. You’d enjoy it more.”

Phainon stared for a moment, then snorted out a sharp, surprised laugh. “Kinky.”

Mydei didn’t flinch. “I’m not joking.”

And he wasn’t.

Phainon could see i, that grim, absolute certainty in Mydei’s gaze. The kind of loyalty that didn’t come with pretty words or gilded oaths, but with sharp edges and the promise of blood.

And for a creature like him, there was nothing in any world more dangerous… or more tempting.

Phainon swallowed hard, his voice a little softer now. “You’re a dangerous man, your highness.”

“You knew what I was when you made the bond.”

“I did,” Phainon murmured. “Still do.”

And gods, if it didn’t make his chest ache in a way no hunger ever had.

The heat of their earlier words lingered in the air between them, but it softened in the quiet that followed. Neither of them spoke for a while, and it was… comfortable. For once.

Phainon let his gaze drift out to the endless expanse before them—the cosmic sea rolling in liquid gold and deep indigos, never ending.

“Mydei,” he murmured after a moment, voice almost a sigh, “your sky’s obscene, you know that?”

Mydei huffed. “Better than the endless dark you nest in.”

“Mm. Debatable.”

The words were nothing, but the quiet proximity meant everything. Their hands brushed once. Then again. Neither pulled away.

Phainon’s fingers shifted, bold and careless as always—but this time, when he let them settle against Mydei’s palm, Mydei didn’t stop him.

Instead, the prince’s fingers curled around his, warm and steady, callused where they had no right to be, considering his title. They stayed like that, wordless, both staring out across the endless sweep of constellations, a pair of dangerous, stubborn creatures pretending for a rare moment to be something softer.

Then it hit.

A pulse in the air—sharp, unsteady, like a string snapping on a lyre. The atmosphere shifted, brittle as cracked glass. Phainon stiffened, a flicker of raw pain arcing through his chest like an old wound split open, though his expression barely changed. Just a blink. A brief twitch of his jaw.

Mydei’s head snapped up. “What was that?”

Phainon gave an excellent performance of casual confusion. “Yeah, what the fuck was that?”

They didn’t have long to wonder.

A figure emerged from one of the side corridors—a young envoy clad in sky-hued armor, breath ragged, a sheen of pale light clinging to his skin. He skidded to a stop a few paces from them and dipped into a hasty bow.

“Highness—apologies. A minor skirmish broke out on the western cusp. One of the celestial tethers destabilized. The wardens are containing it but —”

Mydei’s eyes looked dead. The look he sent the envoy could’ve scoured paint off a temple wall.

“I entrusted half a pantheon’s worth of veterans to manage this convergence,” he said, voice quiet and lethal as a whetted blade. “I assumed I wasn’t presiding over a crèche.”

The envoy paled. “We—we can contain it, your highness. We only thought —”

“Then contain it,” Mydei snapped, standing now, his grip loosening from Phainon’s hand reluctantly. “If you need my direct intervention for a minor tether slip, you’ll need more than a new assignment after this.”

The envoy swallowed hard, bowed again, and all but fled.

Phainon leaned back lazily, though his stomach twisted. The ache was worse now. He wasn’t sure if it was from the instability, the pulse of divine backlash in the air, or the fact that every part of him wanted to drag Mydei back down beside him and keep him there.

“Go on,” he muttered, waving a hand, trying for that causality that didn’t quite land this time. “Your adoring masses need you. I’ll manage.”

Mydei frowned, lingering, studying him. There was something too knowing in his stare.

“I’ll deal with this quickly,” he said at last. “Stay in the sanctum. Rest. And for once,” his gaze narrowed pointedly, “don’t cause a scene.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

“Phainon.”

“What?”

“I mean it.”

“I’ll be good,” Phainon said, throwing up his hands in mock surrender, though his pulse still pounded unpleasantly under his skin.

Mydei held his stare a moment longer, as though contemplating something. Then he turned, his silhouette breaking into a cascade of light, leaving behind only the lingering scent of dusk-warmed marble and incense.

Phainon let his head fall back against the pillar and closed his eyes.

“Yeah,” he muttered to the empty air. “I’m definitely not going to be good.”

Left alone, Phainon let out a slow breath, dragging a hand through his hair like the motion might chase off the ache gnawing at him from the inside out. It didn’t. The air still hummed faintly from whatever celestial tantrum had just ruptured across the firmament, but that wasn’t the problem.

It was him.

It had been him for days. Weeks.

He groaned under his breath, head tipping back. Nearby, a shallow dish sat on a low pedestal—some divine offering, no doubt intended for pious dignitaries or long-dead heroes still waiting on their commemorative title. In it, slices of preserved star-fruit shimmered faintly, each piece veined with thin threads of liquid silver.

Well, fuck it.

He snagged a piece between two fingers, bit down a little too hard. Sweet. Sharp. It burned faintly as it went down, leaving a taste like sugared lightning across his tongue.

Didn’t help.

Of course it didn’t.

He grabbed another, more out of spite than anything else—a petty, childish gesture, like that one time he’d chugged ambrosia straight from the decanter during a famine season and blacked out for three days. A distraction. A rebellion against the gnawing emptiness curling under his ribs and the static itch beneath his skin.

Phainon chewed absently, gaze fixed on the horizon. Distant planets shifted, bent, rippling like liquid—the kind of sight that would’ve left mortals weeping and poets insufferable. To him, it just looked like another far-off problem some poor courtier was scrambling to keep contained.

His stomach twisted again—not from the fruit.

From everything else.

“What the fuck am I doing,” he muttered, to no one.

There was, of course, no answer.

The worst part wasn’t the ache.

It was the other thing. The softer, worse thing.

The way he kept thinking about him.

Phainon groaned again and shoved himself upright, wincing at the sharp crackle beneath his skin, the pull of emptiness clawing down his spine. No one was around to see the tremor in his fingers as he braced them on his thighs, no one to clock the way his breath stuttered, just once.

Fine. He’d go to his room.

Rot there like the tragic cliché he was apparently becoming while Mydei played diplomat to a court of cosmic toddlers.

Decision made, Phainon turned on his heel, grabbing one more slice of whatever-the-hell divine fruit for the road. Might as well. If the realm was going to kill him, it could at least feed him on the way out.

And that was the thing about Mydei’s sanctum—a stronghold carved from starstone and blood, decked in impossible light and skies that moved when no one was looking.

It let you fall apart in absolute, unapologetic style.

He didn’t quite make it to his room.

The halls twisted in lazy spirals, corridors unfurling like silk ribbons in the dark. Phainon barely registered the turn his feet took, too dulled by hunger to bother correcting course.

It wasn’t until a pulse slid along his senses—sharp, wrong, and gone too quick—that his steps slowed.

He blinked, straightening, frowning into the hush. The place was ancient, its bones older than the gods themselves if the songs could be trusted. It breathed, sometimes. Shifted. Let its thresholds move like drifting tides. But this… this wasn’t the usual groaning of restless foundations or the static haze of converging ley-lines.

This was something waking.

Phainon huffed out a sigh, dragging a hand down his face. “For fuck’s sake,” he muttered, voice gravel against the velvet dark. “He tells me not to cause a scene and then leaves me with this.”

But it was his home, too. In all its impossible, gilded vastness—this realm of Mydei’s—it had cradled his worse nights and stitched his broken pieces together more than once. He wasn’t about to let some half-assed tremor slip by without a look.

He veered left. Down a corridor where the torches guttered in shades of blue and violet, their flames licking at the air like restless tongues. The further he went, the thicker the air felt—not oppressive, but stretched.

The pulse came again.

Faint.

“Alright, alright,” Phainon grumbled, stretching his arms as he moved. “Let’s see what you’re about.”

It led him deeper. Past vaults of sealed antiques, rooms whose names had been forgotten before the earth cooled. At some point, the sanctum’s elegant geometry frayed, corridors breaking into strange, slanted pathways that coiled back on themselves. It wasn’t disorienting to him—the place had always bent a little easier for his tread. But the sense of wrongness gnawed sharp at his nerves.

Eventually, the path outpaced his patience.

The next ledge broke into open air—a drop into one of the lower terraces. Phainon didn’t hesitate. He vaulted over the edge, catching a hanging arch with one hand, shoes skimming a sun disc’s rim as he swung down. A series of shallow landings spiraled below, and he dropped through them with ease —a flick of movement here, a reckless bound there, until the pulse in the air thickened and drew him toward another archway half-concealed behind a sweep of golden tendrils.

It was old.

One of the Syzygy Gates—high arched, carved with runes he couldn’t read. A construct meant to link realms during the great convergences, when the veils between worlds thinned like gold leaf under a knife. This one should’ve been dead, sealed by god knows who, left to gather dust and moss in its cradle of stone.

But here it was.

Flickering.

Not fully active, but not fully dormant either. A thin line of argent luminescence hummed along the curve of its frame, like a half-drawn breath.

“Well, shit.”

Phainon scrubbed a hand through his hair, the glow from the gate painting pale streaks across his skin. He could leave it. Should leave it. Some overeager legate probably fumbled a containment ward. It would fizzle out once the convergence waned, no harm done.

Except…

His gaze snagged on the passage beside it. A connecting space—not a chamber, but one of the Hypourania Courts. A liminal place between thresholds, where the oldest of the sanctum’s powers once gathered to

broker pacts and blood-oaths. He’d heard about them, sure. Mydei mentioned them in passing once, dismissing them as relics of a bloodier age. Most were sealed, their entrances bricked over with starstone, threads of ancient law binding their thresholds.

This one wasn’t.

A thin seam of shadow cut along its frame, a sliver of space just wide enough for a reckless, half-delirious bastard to slip through.

Which he did.

Because of course he did.

The air inside tasted different. Cooler. It smelled like hollowed-out altars, the ghost of burnt offerings clinging to the walls. The floor was inlaid with patterns—lines of silver, arcs of obsidian dust, constellations carved into the stone beneath his feet.

Phainon paused, a flicker of unease crawling along his ribs.

“Okay,” he said to the dark, voice low. “If something in here plans on chewing on my spleen, now’s your chance.”

No answer.

He moved forward.

And what little light there was coalesced ahead—a distant, hovering glow, tangled in the roots of some ancient sigil, half-erased but still seething. The convergence had stirred it. Drawn thin cracks in the old seals.

Phainon cocked his head, watching the light throb against the dark like a dying ember. He didn’t know what it was. Didn’t especially want to know.

But he was already here.

And it wasn’t like anyone was watching.

He made his way through the gloom, boots scuffing against mosaic patterns. Fragments of scripture curled along the walls, half-devoured by creeping roots. He moved like a shadow through it, every bone in his body tensed, throat dry, pulse a slow, leaden drum.

It was the mirror that stopped him.

Not a mirror, not really. Just a basin of viscous, silvery ichor, thick as liquid moonlight. The surface churned without wind, reflecting nothing until one dared to look.

Once, the immortals stared into these depths, before they forged their heavens and chained their own wildness. They looked upon the thing no worshiper was meant to see.

Phainon caught a flicker of movement, his own reflection snagging on the ichor’s restless gleam.

And what stared back wasn’t him.

Not as he was.

The thing in the ichor was gaunt, ravenous, eyes bright with a starved, sharp hunger that no wine or violence or careless kiss could slake. Its lips pulled back from bloodstained teeth in something too close to a grin. Its throat worked as if swallowing something thick and hot. A dozen smears of stolen touch, of fire, of iron tang and salt sweat clung to its skin like war paint.

It mouthed something.

He didn’t catch it. Didn’t want to.

Phainon whistled low, like one does to an animal too dangerous to startle. But his hand gripped the edge of the basin, fingers white-knuckled on cold stone.

Don’t look at me like that.

He told it nothing.

It didn’t matter. The Court was listening.

He forced himself to straighten, tried to shake the heaviness from his limbs, muttering some half-hearted curse about Mydei’s insufferable taste in décor as he turned—and saw it.

A fragment.

Leaning against a toppled column of veined marble, half-buried in dust and crumbling silk. A shard of crystal—not much larger than a palm’s width, but the moment his gaze caught it, a pulse bloomed sharp behind his eyes.

The Erotheion Lens.

The resonance gave it away before his eyes did. Not a weapon—a vessel of longing, wrought to transmute lust into covenant. This was a lens made for rites where sovereigns and gods spilled themselves into one another beneath a darkened sky. It did not merely reflect desire. It bore it aloft. And though fractured by time and the trembling of the convergence, its pulse still clung to him like a lover’s touch.

It recognized him.

The moment Phainon stepped near, the fragment flared.

A pulse—a sickeningly sweet ache that sank straight through his ribs and coiled tight around the meat of him. It wasn’t a feeling. It was a bite. A hook driven beneath his sternum, dragging something raw and bleeding into the open.

And before he could brace, his restraint—brittle, overdrawn, already fraying since Aetheris began—snapped.

It wasn’t a clean break. It was a void. A yawning, lightless, marrow-deep hunger that swallowed him whole.

It hit like a rupture, like his insides turned inside out. His stomach clenched, breath stuttered, vision searing sharp and bright, then dim. Not just for blood. Not just for touch. Not even for Mydei, though gods, the thought of

him—sun-warm, eyes like stormbreak, the pale line of his throat bared without knowing—burned through Phainon’s mind so violently it left him unsteady.

No. It was for everything.

For divinity. For ruin. For the ache of flesh under his palm. For the weight of a soul dragged screaming from its shell. For the taste of iron, the press of skin, the crash of a name torn from a throat. For worship. For desecration. Holy and profane. Beautiful and defiled.

His knees nearly gave. A dry sound cracked from his throat.

“—no.”

But the Court heard him.

The damn thing was alive. And it was starving.

For the ache in his marrow, for the black curl of need, for the thing gnashing beneath his tongue every time he bit it down. It unspooled every brittle wall he’d raised, peeled them back like wet parchment, left his hungers naked, thrashing.

His reflection in the ichor twisted, grinned.

He felt his hand tremble. Clenched his fist tight enough for nails to bite skin.

“Stop.” The word barely made it out. A rasp, a plea, a command.

The Court thrummed. It wasn’t going to let him leave standing.

And he felt it. If he lingered, even a heartbeat longer, it would strip him bare. Leave him some howling, hollow thing, a creature of want and nothing else.

He swayed, breath ragged, the world tilting in hot, colorless waves.

He hadn’t meant to come here. Hadn’t meant to wake it. Hadn’t meant to turn himself inside out on ancient teeth.

But it was done.

Now or never.

Phainon tore himself away.

It wasn’t graceful. His body moved before his mind could catch up— staggering back from the ichor’s surface, from the Lens’ cracked glow, from the grasping ache of the Court’s pulse.

He didn’t remember the door. Only the sensation under his palm as he shoved past the cold threshold, the feeling of the place watching him, a low, mocking hum beneath his ribs.

The Hypourania Courts felt amused.

Like something vast and ravenous had cracked open one lidded eye, seen him laid bare, and found the sight laughable.

By the time he reached the outer passage, his breath was ragged, his skin clammy. The light of the Celestialis—so soft and sacred on better days—hit like knives, every gleam and glimmer searing too bright against his eyes. The air smelled too sharp, too sweet, cloying with incense and sun-warmed stone, the heady perfume of immortals and old rites clinging to him like a second skin.

His pace faltered.

Phainon pitched sideways, shoulder hitting a column. His vision ghosted at the edges, his pulse a drumbeat in his skull. He brought his wrist to his mouth, bit down hard, teeth breaking skin, copper blooming hot and metallic on his tongue. The pain barely cut through.

It didn’t ground him.

It only reminded him how close it had gotten.

Blood welled, smeared over his palm as he pushed off the column, not sparing a glance for the figure or two that might’ve turned their heads. He didn’t care. He couldn’t. Every shape blurred into the same too-sharp smear of color and heat. The Celestialis itself felt like it was pressing in, narrow and endless at once, the air thickening with every step.

His pace stuttered, then picked up.

He didn’t remember choosing to run, but his legs moved on their own— desperate, fevered, an animal in retreat. And the farther he fled, the deeper the itch in his bones crawled, like the Court’s pulse had left a handprint beneath his skin.

He was wrong. He’d made a mistake.

A bad one.

He reached his chambers in a blur of half-sensed turns and blurred thresholds, the world around him a smear of too-sharp light and cloying air. The door was an arch of sigil-burnt stone, and he shoved it shut with the full weight of his body. The wards flared, ancient seals threading through the air like spun glass, latching into place with a soundless finality.

The moment the last tether cinched tight, it hit him.

No courtly mask, no feigned composure, no thin, aching restraint. The thing inside him—old, hungering, wrought of silk and thorn and flesh’s darker wants—surged to the surface like a wave breaking over a drowning man.

His skin burned. Flushed fever-warm, fever-wrong. His pulse a frantic, shuddering drum against his ribs. Breath hitched, sharp, shallow, ragged. Sweat clung to him, salt and heat and something acrid beneath it. His pupils, already dark, blew wide, swallowing the world. Teeth ached in his skull—too sharp, too eager. His mouth was dry and slick all at once.

Every breath tasted like the Courts. Like ichor and desire and blood-warm air.

He staggered, palm catching the nearest wall, a growl ghosting his lips.

He was fine.

Totally fine.

This was—part of the plan. A calculated risk. He’d… he’d accounted for this.

Phainon muttered it like a mantra, half-mad as he tore at his collar, the clasps refusing him for a heartbeat before giving way. His skin felt too tight, every breath like knives. Cold water burned. Warm scalded. Nothing soothed. He gripped the basin’s edge until his knuckles whitened, splashing water over his face that steamed on contact, hissing as it met fevered flesh.

“You’re fine,” he rasped, voice cracking. “Just… ride it out. It’ll pass.”

But it didn’t.

Mydei’s face bled through his mind unbidden—the impossible softness of him, thunderlight catching in his eyes, the way his throat bared without fear. Hands around Phainon’s wrists like shackles made of grace.

He made a ragged sound, half a laugh, half a snarl.

Something moved in the reflection.

Not him.

Or rather—him, but other. Eyes like wells, mouth curling in a knowing, cruel slant.

“Hungry, little incubi?”

The voice wasn’t his own.

Phainon lunged. Fist through glass, or what passed for it. The surface shattered in a burst of lightless shards, the voice shattering with it. Ichor-light bled from the break.

Breathing hard, hand bloodied, he pressed his forehead to the stone.

He was fine.

He was fine.

He was so completely, irreversibly, fucked.

The hours after were a blur. Phainon barely remembered how he got from the broken reflection to his bed—if you could call it that. More a ruin of silken sheets now, bloodied where his knuckles split, sweat-damp, twisted around his limbs like some half-hearted shroud.

He’d buried himself in it, trembling in the aftermath, skin flushed and fevered, pulse a hammerbeat in his throat. Every nerve felt flayed raw.

And then—

“Phainon.”

A sharp knock. A voice he knew too well.

“If you don’t let me in, I swear by every star in your rotten veins, I’m breaking this fucking door down.”

Phainon groaned, dragging a hand down his face. Of course. Of course.

“Mydei…” he croaked, half-muffled in a pillow. “Go away. I’m… meditating.”

“You’re full of shit.”

Another hard knock. Phainon winced.

“I’m fine,” he tried, though it came out more like a pained whimper.

“Yeah, you’re so fine you barricaded your chambers and sent half the realm’s wards into a panic,” Mydei shot back, exasperated. “I felt what

happened in the Hypourania Courts, you idiot. Did you really think you could pull whatever that was and I wouldn’t notice?”

Phainon rolled onto his side, burying his face deeper into the twisted sheets. Gods, even Mydei’s voice made his skin prickle.

“Seriously, you don’t want to be in here right now,” he ground out. “I’m… it’s bad, Mydei.”

A pause. Then, softer: “I know.”

Phainon cursed under his breath.

He could imagine the look on Mydei’s face—somewhere between murder and worry. It made something in his chest hurt.

“Just give me… a minute. Or an hour. Or a decade.”

“Phainon.”

“Not helping.”

He could practically hear Mydei crossing his arms through the door.

A beat passed. Then, lightly: “You’re an idiot.”

Phainon let out a ragged laugh despite himself, scrubbing at his face.

“Yeah,” he muttered, closing his eyes, trying—failing—to slow his heartbeat. “I know.”

And because he had no strength left for dignity, he sighed and sank deeper into the mess of pillows and sheets.

“…Don’t come in yet though, seriously. I might actually devour you.”

“Noted.”

But Mydei didn’t leave. Just leaned against the door, waiting.

Phainon hated how much comfort that brought.

“…You shouldn’t have come.”

Outside, a beat of silence.

Then, steady as a vow, “I always do.”

Phainon let out a breath. He should’ve left it there. Let the moment pass, let Mydei’s stubbornness settle like it always did. But the ache in his ribs twisted sharp, and a sound slipped from his throat—not quite a curse, not quite a whimper, but unmistakably pain.

The silence shattered.

“Mydei—wait, it’s fine—”

“Phainon.”

The name was no longer a gentle tether, it was a snapped thread.

Then came the pressure—a ripple through the wards, the ancient seals set by his own hand. The sanctum shuddered under it, light fracturing along the archways, the sigils burning briefly gold.

Even here, even behind every layer of Incubi-spun barriers and possession wards, Mydei’s will pressed against his own like a rising tide.

Phainon flinched, teeth gritting as another wave of ache surged through him.

“Don’t.” he rasped. “It’s locked for a reason, Mydei.”

“I gave you patience,” Mydei’s voice wasn’t angry, but it carried the steady authority of one born to command. “I gave you mercy.”

The seals hissed against the strain. A second longer and he’d speak the words that would undo them, would bind Phainon’s will to his own, as was his right here in the Celestialis.

Phainon, delirious or not, knew it the moment it started—the old invocation rising in Mydei’s voice.

“I give you a command—”

“Wait, wait!” Phainon croaked, a rough, breathless laugh breaking through as he curled tighter against the ache in his belly. “That’s cheating, Mydei.”

A beat. Then the weight at the door stilled—not gone, but balanced, held on the edge of yielding.

“Then open it yourself,” Mydei said, quieter now, but no less unmovable. “Or I will.”

Phainon let his head fall back against the pillows, half laughing, half sobbing.

“You’re impossible.”

“I’ve heard,” Mydei murmured, and if there was fondness in it, Phainon didn’t have the strength to shove it away.

Another long breath. Another crack in the walls he’d built.

“Don’t—” Phainon started, then faltered, pressing his hand over his chest where the hunger still clawed. “It’s… worse than before.”

“I know,” came the reply. “I felt it.”

A pause. Even a Crown Prince had to bleed to breach a sanctum like this— but Mydei was already halfway there, and Phainon could feel the bond between them humming tight and thin.

“Let me in, Phainon.”

Phainon swallowed hard.

“I shouldn’t,” he whispered.

“I didn’t ask if you should.”

The final wards buckled, seals cracking like brittle bone under the weight of the Crown Prince’s will. A rush of incense-thick air met Mydei as he crossed the threshold—as though the room itself mourned its master’s state.

He stepped through like strength given flesh, eyes sharp, mantle burning faintly at his shoulders. And then —

He saw him.

Phainon lay tangled in sweat-damp sheets, blood staining the linen, his skin flushed and too pale by turns, hair clinging to his brow, throat marked where his own nails had scratched. A creature unmade by his own hungers.

And in an instant, every ounce of princely detachment left Mydei’s face.

He was at the bedside before the thought had finished forming, the heavy fall of his robes pooling around him as he dropped to his knees, a hand already cupping Phainon’s cheek, thumb brushing against burning skin.

“Phainon…” Mydei’s voice cracked low with it—frustration and fear and something else.

“I told you,” Mydei muttered, the anger brittle, made of care. “I told you to stay out of trouble, I told you this would happen—”

Phainon laughed—a hoarse, broken sound. “Yeah, well…” he rasped, head lolling against the pillow, half-dazed, half-miserable. “I’ve always been shit at listening.”

And then, as though the heat in his chest had turned his tongue reckless, the words slipped.

“It was easier before you.”

The moment hung, heavy and terrible. Phainon’s eyes squeezed shut, breath ragged. “Forget it. Ignore me. Gods, just—just forget it.”

But Mydei didn’t move.

A beat. Then, softer than it should’ve been, “No.”

His thumb brushed the corner of Phainon’s mouth, eyes still fixed on his face, unwavering.

“I’m listening.”

Phainon let out a sound—sharp, wrecked, half a laugh, half a breath like a sob. His fingers dug into his own arms as though he could hold himself together by force. Mydei’s hand was still there, warm against his jaw, and it burned.

He should’ve pulled away.

He should’ve told him to leave.

But the words wouldn’t come out. Not the ones he was supposed to say.

Instead what came was:

“You don’t know what it’s like,” Phainon spat, voice hoarse. “You—you can’t. You wake up every morning and the world fucking belongs to you. The sun sings for you, the storms clear for you, the gods bend for you. You get to be righteous, you get to be good.”

His throat worked around a bitter, broken laugh.

“And me? I wake up hungry. Every. Fucking. Day. Wanting things I shouldn’t, craving things that make the everyone flinch. And I choke it down. I bury it. I play nice, and I smile, and I let them laugh like I’m some —some harmless pretty thing and I let them, because if I don’t, they’ll see me for what I am.”

He sucked in a breath, ragged, his voice cracking on the next words.

“I didn’t ask to be this. I didn’t ask to want like this. I didn’t ask to have to crawl through every day pretending I don’t wanna tear the world apart just

to feel full for once.”

His vision blurred, chest heaving like his ribs would split apart. He pressed his palm hard against his sternum, trying to push it all back down, but it was too late.

“And I—” his voice dropped to a choked whisper, eyes flicking up to Mydei’s. “I wanted you to see me. And I hate you for it. Because you did. And now you’re here and I—”

He cut himself off, shaking his head, a forced sigh breaking over. “Gods. Just—just fucking ignore me. I didn’t mean it. None of it. Just… go.”

Mydei didn’t speak at first.

For a beat, he just stared—as if Phainon’s words had knocked the breath from him, left something hairline-cracked behind his steady gaze. His mouth parted, then closed again, a dozen replies stifling themselves at the back of his throat.

And then—softer than Phainon would’ve expected—Mydei’s voice broke the air between them.

“…I didn’t know,” he murmured, and it wasn’t a defense. It sounded like an admission. A failure. His hand lifted, hesitated in the space between them, fingers curling once like he wasn’t sure if he was allowed. Then—slowly, carefully—he let his palm rest against the side of Phainon’s neck, a tether, not a chain.

“I didn’t… I should’ve seen it,” Mydei said, his voice catching on the words, guilt pooling in the spaces between them. “I thought—” He cut himself off, shaking his head, a humorless huff of breath leaving him. “I didn’t stop to think. I just told myself you were fine—because you always act like you are. And I let that be enough.”

He swallowed hard, his thumb brushing against Phainon’s skin like he could smooth the ache away.

“And that was easier for me.”

A breath hung between them. The quiet kind of ache.

“I’m sorry,” Mydei said at last. Not loud, not grand, but raw. Honest. “I’m sorry I left you to deal with this on your own. For not seeing it. For not asking when I should’ve.”

His hand tightened at Phainon’s nape, grounding him in place as if anchoring them both.

“I should’ve known,” Mydei whispered, voice thick. “And if it’s not too late —I’m here now.”

Phainon made a sound then—small, splintered, barely a breath—and Mydei inched closer, their foreheads nearly brushing, the air between them charged and trembling.

“I’m not leaving,” Mydei said, lower now. A promise. A quiet, breaking vow. “You don’t have to preten. Not with me.”

Phainon’s face crumpled. His body shuddered, his hands fisting in the fabric at his knees like he could stop the unraveling, but it was too late. The dam broke.

And this time, when he tipped forward, burying his face in the crook of Mydei’s shoulder, Mydei caught him.

Held him like something precious.

Like something long overdue.
